title: Mid-stream exception loses `type`/`code` when the exception block is split across stream chunks (`extractErrorAtTheEndOfChunk`)
body:
**Versions:** `@clickhouse/client` 1.18.2 (also checked: the code is unchanged in 1.24.1). Server: ClickHouse
26.3.59.10 (any version ≥ 25.11 that sends `X-ClickHouse-Exception-Tag`). Node 24.

### What happens

When a query throws after rows were streamed (`JSONEachRow`), the server appends an exception block framed by the
exception tag, then drops the connection:

```
<rows>\r\n__exception__\r\n<tag>\r\n<message>\n<len(message)+1> <tag>\r\n__exception__\r\n
```

`ResultSet.stream()` (and therefore `json()`) checks each chunk for the first `\r\n`, and on finding it calls
`extractErrorAtTheEndOfChunk(chunk, exceptionTag)`, which reads the length field backwards **from the end of that
chunk**. If a socket read boundary falls inside the block, the chunk's end is not the block's end, and the client
rejects with a plain `Error`. The message is either `there was an error in the stream; failed to parse the message
length` or a fragment of the server message, and there is no `type` or `code`. With the whole block in one chunk,
the same body gives a proper `ClickHouseError` (`type: 'FUNCTION_THROW_IF_VALUE_IS_NON_ZERO'`, `code: '395'`).

In practice this is intermittent: it depends on how the kernel hands the response to Node, and it shows up under
load (we saw it on roughly every other CI run on a busy runner).

### Minimal reproduction (no network timing needed)

1. Capture a real body:

   ```sh
   curl -s "http://localhost:8123/?max_block_size=1000&param_v=placeholder" \
     --data "SELECT number, throwIf(number = 2000, concat('v ', {v:String})) FROM numbers(100000) FORMAT JSONEachRow" \
     -D headers.txt -o body.bin
   ```

   `headers.txt` has `X-ClickHouse-Exception-Tag: <tag>`.

2. Feed it to a real `ResultSet` as two chunks, cut at every offset around the block:

   ```js
   const { ResultSet } = require('@clickhouse/client')
   const { Readable } = require('node:stream')
   const body = require('node:fs').readFileSync('body.bin')
   const tag = '<tag from headers.txt>'
   const start = body.indexOf('\r\n__exception__')
   for (let cut = start - 5; cut <= body.length; cut++) {
     const chunks = [body.subarray(0, cut), body.subarray(cut)].filter((c) => c.length > 0)
     const rs = ResultSet.instance({
       stream: Readable.from(chunks),
       format: 'JSONEachRow',
       query_id: 'q',
       log_error: () => {},
       response_headers: { 'x-clickhouse-exception-tag': tag },
     })
     const err = await rs.json().catch((e) => e)
     console.log(cut - start, err.constructor.name, err.type, err.code)
   }
   ```

3. Result for a 419-byte block: cuts at block offsets **2 to 418** (417 of 419) give a plain `Error` with
   `type`/`code` undefined. Cuts at offsets ≤ 1, or no cut, give the `ClickHouseError` with type and code.

### Expected

The exception is parsed from the whole block whatever the chunking, so `type` and `code` are always set.

### Suggested fix

When the transform sees the block's start (`\r\n__exception__\r\n<tag>\r\n`), buffer from there until the closing
`<tag>\r\n__exception__\r\n` arrives, then parse the buffered block. Don't wait for the stream to end: the server
drops the connection right after the closing marker, so the response never emits `end`. (We work around it on our
side by holding back the response tail and releasing it as one chunk on the closing marker.)

### Related

- #976 covers the paths that never look for the exception block (`ResultSet.text()`, `exec()`). Single-document
  `format: 'JSON'` goes through the same text path, so it loses `type`/`code` in the same way (the caller sees the
  connection drop, `ECONNRESET` "aborted").
- #974 is a different defect in the same function (any `\r\n` in the body triggers the detector), and #607 looks like
  a symptom of it. This issue is about valid exception blocks that are split across chunks; fixing one doesn't fix
  the other, but a fix that only starts buffering on the full opening marker and parses at the closing marker would likely address both.

title: feat: send the query() format as default_format instead of appending FORMAT
body:
## Summary

`query()` now sends the user's SQL as written and passes its `format` to the server as the `default_format` setting, instead of trimming the query, stripping trailing semicolons and appending `\nFORMAT <format>`. This is how the Go, Rust and Java clients work. Closes #1079.

It fixes the problems caused by the appended clause:

- a semicolon followed by a comment (`SELECT 1; -- note`) no longer fails with `Multi-statements are not allowed` (#973);
- `FORMAT` is no longer placed after a trailing `SETTINGS` clause (#970);
- the short `SHOW ROW POLICIES` syntax works (#759).

`command()` and `exec()` also send the SQL as written, except `exec()` with `values`, where trailing semicolons are still removed because the server reads the data right after the statement.

## Observable changes

- The `format` option overrides a `default_format` in `clickhouse_settings`.
- The query text in `system.query_log`, logs and traces no longer ends with `FORMAT`.
- **A `FORMAT` clause inside a `query()` query:** the server prefers it over `default_format`, so the response could be parsed with the wrong format. `query()` now compares the `X-ClickHouse-Format` response header with the `format` option and throws an error naming both when they differ. A matching clause is accepted. Statements without output do not send the header and are unaffected. (Before, this was always a duplicate-`FORMAT` syntax error.)
- **A user profile that locks `default_format`** (a `<constraints>` entry) now fails every `query()` with `SETTING_CONSTRAINT_VIOLATION`, because `default_format` is sent on every request. Seen on 26.10 and 26.11; 24.8 and 23.8 reject `default_format` in a profile, so it cannot happen there. Mentioned in the changelogs and covered by an integration test.
- **An `X-ClickHouse-Format` request header** set via `http_headers` (client or call level) is not sent by `query()`: the server prefers it over `default_format` (and, on 26.8+, over an inline `FORMAT`), so it would make the response unparseable. The other methods send it as given.
- **Errors on 24.8:** an error raised before execution comes back through the JSON-family output formats (`{"exception": ...}`, a whole document with an `exception` key, `["..."]`, ...), where it used to be plain text because the appended `FORMAT` was inside the query that failed to parse. `parseError()` now extracts the text so `ClickHouseError.message` keeps no JSON escaping. Plain-text formats (CSV, TSV, Parquet, ...) are unaffected. The same applies, on every version, to an error raised while the result is written (`http_write_exception_in_output_format`): the exception row then comes after the column names, types and data rows, and `parseError()` picks the first candidate that parses as a ClickHouse error.

## Testing

- Integration tests run a failing query for every `DataFormat` on both clients. They pass on 26.11 and on 24.8.14; without the `parseError` change, the 14 JSON-family formats fail on 24.8.
- The header handling and the mid-stream error parsing were also run against 24.8.14 and 26.11 for every JSON format with both clients.
- The CI matrix does not include 24.8, so the 24.8 behaviour is not covered in CI. This is tracked separately.

## #1087

The format-mismatch error closes the result set, which needed the `ResultSet.close()` fix from #1087 (Node.js). It is merged, and `main` was merged into this branch.

## Checklist

- [x] Unit and integration tests covering the common scenarios were added
- [x] A human-readable changelog entry was added to every affected package's `CHANGELOG.md` (`client-node` and `client-web`)
- [x] For significant changes, documentation in https://github.com/ClickHouse/clickhouse-docs was updated with further explanations or tutorials

title: fix: parse exception blocks split across stream chunks
body:
## Summary

When a query fails after rows were streamed, ClickHouse 25.11+ appends a tagged exception block to the response (the tag comes from `X-ClickHouse-Exception-Tag`):

```
<rows>\r\n__exception__\r\n<tag>\r\n<message>\n<len> <tag>\r\n__exception__\r\n
```

If a chunk boundary fell anywhere inside this block, `ResultSet.stream()` / `ResultSet.json()` failed with a plain `Error` with no `code` or `type` (`failed to parse the message length`, or a piece of the server message) instead of a `ClickHouseError`. This affects both `@clickhouse/client` and `@clickhouse/client-web`.

Fixes #1084

## Root cause

Both transforms looked for the first `\n` preceded by `\r`, then called `extractErrorAtTheEndOfChunk(chunk, tag)` right away. That function reads the length field backwards from the end of **the current chunk**, which only works when the chunk ends exactly where the block ends. Two smaller problems in the same path:

- If the `\r` of the opening `\r\n` was the last byte of the previous chunk, the check never matched at all. The `\r` became an ordinary row, and the block was then parsed from the next chunk.
- The backward newline scan in `extractErrorAtTheEndOfChunk` had no lower bound. On some truncated blocks (for example a chunk that ends right after `\r\n__ex`) it went past index 0 and looped forever.

## Fix

- New `ExceptionBlockBuffer` in `client-common/src/utils/stream.ts`, used by both the Node and the Web `ResultSet.stream()`. Once the start of the block is seen, the transform hands all remaining bytes to it. It checks the opening `\r\n__exception__\r\n<tag>` as soon as those bytes arrive, keeps collecting until the closing `<tag>\r\n__exception__\r\n` shows up, and only then calls `extractErrorAtTheEndOfChunk` on the complete block. It does not wait for the stream to end, because the server drops the connection right after the closing marker.
- Buffering has a limit. Normal row data is handled as before. The buffer starts only at an `\r\n` row boundary, fails as soon as the bytes stop matching the opening marker (at most 34 bytes for a 16-character tag), and stops at 16 KiB, which is the server's `MAX_EXCEPTION_SIZE` for the whole block.
- The transforms also detect the block when the `\r` was the last byte of the previous chunk.
- Rows parsed earlier in the same chunk are still pushed while the transform waits for the rest of the block.
- If the response ends before the closing marker arrives, the stream now fails with `there was an error in the stream, but the exception block is malformed or incomplete`. Before, it either failed with a misparsed error or hung.
- The backward scan in `extractErrorAtTheEndOfChunk` now stops at index 0 and returns the existing "malformed" error.

Out of scope: #974 / #976 (false positives on an `\r\n` in row data, and the `text()` / `exec()` paths). A wrong `\r\n` still fails the stream, same as before. It now fails within the length of the opening marker, without trying to parse the bytes.

## How tested

New unit tests, no server needed:

- `packages/client-node/__tests__/unit/node_result_set_exception_block.test.ts` and `packages/client-web/__tests__/unit/web_result_set_exception_block.test.ts` (4 tests each). The body is 2 `JSONEachRow` rows plus a 293-byte exception block in the exact server framing, with a 16-character tag. The tests check:
  - the block in one chunk;
  - the body split in two at **every** byte offset (322 cuts), each asserting `ClickHouseError` with `code: "395"`, `type: "FUNCTION_THROW_IF_VALUE_IS_NON_ZERO"` and the message;
  - every byte as its own chunk;
  - the response truncated at every offset inside the block (291 points × 2 chunkings), which must fail with an Error and must not hang.
- `packages/client-common/__tests__/unit/stream_utils.test.ts` (+6 tests): `ExceptionBlockBuffer` with the whole block, byte-by-byte input, a wrong opening marker, a wrong tag, the 16 KiB limit, and the `extractErrorAtTheEndOfChunk` input that used to loop forever.

Before the fix, the two-way split test fails first at block offset 2 (the same result as in the issue), the byte-per-chunk test fails with `SyntaxError: Unexpected end of JSON input`, and the truncation test hangs (infinite loop).

Results with the fix:

- `npm run test:node:unit`: 45 files, 412 passed, 10 skipped
- `npm run test:web:unit` (Chromium): 27 files, 267 passed
- `tsc --noEmit` and `eslint --max-warnings=0` pass for `client-common`, `client-node` and `client-web`; `prettier --check` is clean

## Checklist

- [x] Unit and integration tests covering the common scenarios were added (unit only; the chunking can't be controlled reliably against a real server)
- [x] A human-readable changelog entry was added to every affected package's `CHANGELOG.md` (`client-node` 1.24.2, `client-web` 1.24.1)

title: fix(client-node): do not throw the closure error as uncaught from ResultSet.close()
body:
## Summary

`ResultSet.close()` in the Node.js client destroys the response stream with a `ResultSet has been closed` error. If the wrapped stream has no `error` listener, Node.js throws that error as an uncaught exception, which can crash the process. The error only signals the closure, so a no-op `error` listener is now attached before the stream is destroyed. Repeated `close()` calls are a no-op once the stream is destroyed, so they do not keep adding listeners.

For a stream produced by the client itself this was already safe: the request-level `error` handler in `socket_pool.ts` absorbs the error for a raw `IncomingMessage` (Node.js forwards it to the `ClientRequest`, not the response), and `Stream.pipeline` attaches its own listeners for a decompressed response. The fix covers a `ResultSet` wrapping any other stream, and hardens `close()` so that it does not depend on the caller having wired up a listener.

This is needed by #1085, whose new format-mismatch error in `query()` closes the result set. It is split out so that it can be merged first.

## Checklist

- [x] Unit and integration tests covering the common scenarios were added
- [x] A human-readable changelog entry was added to every affected package's `CHANGELOG.md` (`client-node` only: the Web `ResultSet.close()` uses `cancel()` and is not affected)
- [ ] For significant changes, documentation in https://github.com/ClickHouse/clickhouse-docs was updated with further explanations or tutorials (not relevant)

Release notes

v8.12.3

What's Changed

  • build(deps-dev): bump neostandard from 0.13.0 to 0.14.0 by @​dependabot[bot] in nodejs/undici#6006
  • build(deps-dev): bump eslint from 9.39.4 to 10.12.0 by @​dependabot[bot] in nodejs/undici#5967

Full Changelog: https://github.com/nodejs/undici/compare/v8.12.2...v8.12.3

v8.12.2

Security fixes

High severity

Denial of service via TLS 1.2 certificate-changing renegotiation

CVE-2026-87018 · GHSA-qrxm-fqhp-jwvm

A malicious or compromised HTTPS server could crash the Node.js process by initiating TLS 1.2 renegotiation and presenting a different, CA-trusted certificate whose hostname did not match the requested host. The resulting socket error reached an assertion in undici's HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 connection handling. This release handles post-connect certificate errors without terminating the process.

TLS certificate validation bypass through dropped Agent options

CVE-2026-109383 · GHSA-2m5v-pch6-74hx

Agent used a JSON-based clone for constructor options, which silently removed function-valued TLS options such as checkServerIdentity. Applications relying on custom certificate or public-key verification could therefore accept a certificate that the callback was intended to reject. This release preserves TLS options when creating per-origin dispatchers.

Cache poisoning and cross-user disclosure through cross-origin redirects

CVE-2026-109829 · GHSA-4w7w-5xrc-9h26

When an originless Agent combined redirect and shared-cache interceptors as compose(redirect(), cache()), a response from a cross-origin redirect could be stored under the original URL. This could allow persistent cache poisoning or disclosure of user-specific responses to later callers. This release verifies the response origin before caching and preserves redirect-hop cache-control policy.

Denial of service through excessive Content-Encoding values

CVE-2026-109869 · GHSA-xjj6-f33q-929c

A malicious HTTP server could crash the Node.js process by returning more than five content codings and closing the connection before sending the body. Although fetch() rejected the response, an error from an orphaned internal stream could remain unhandled. This release validates the content-encoding chain before creating the body stream and aborts oversized chains safely.

Medium severity

Denial of service through the decompress interceptor

CVE-2026-87029 · GHSA-55wc-3pg8-jfw6

This release preserves TLS options when creating per-origin dispatchers.

Cache poisoning and cross-user disclosure through cross-origin redirects

CVE-2026-109829 · GHSA-4w7w-5xrc-9h26

When an originless Agent combined redirect and shared-cache interceptors as compose(redirect(), cache()), a response from a cross-origin redirect could be stored under the original URL. This could allow persistent cache poisoning or disclosure of user-specific responses to later callers. This release verifies the response origin before caching and preserves redirect-hop cache-control policy.

Denial of service through excessive Content-Encoding values

CVE-2026-109869 · GHSA-xjj6-f33q-929c

A malicious HTTP server could crash the Node.js process by returning more than five content codings and closing the connection before sending the body. Although fetch() rejected the response, an error from an orphaned internal stream could remain unhandled. This release validates the content-encoding chain before creating the body stream and aborts oversized chains safely.

Medium severity

Denial of service through the decompress interceptor

CVE-2026-87029 · GHSA-55wc-3pg8-jfw6

An exception thrown by a downstream response handler from an asynchronous decompression callback could escape as an uncaught exception. A server could trigger this when decompress was composed with a handler such as dump with a size limit. This release converts downstream handler exceptions into per-request errors.

Subresource Integrity bypass with non-lowercase algorithm tokens

CVE-2026-109841 · GHSA-f72v-6w45-q472

fetch() treated valid mixed-case or uppercase SRI algorithm tokens, such as SHA256, as unknown and could accept a response whose body did not match the configured digest. This release normalizes algorithm tokens before validation and digest selection.

Denial of service through unbounded EventSource parser state

CVE-2026-109924 · GHSA-4qv8-2p9j-2685

A malicious Server-Sent Events endpoint could exhaust process memory by sending many tiny data: fields without completing an event, or by splitting an unfinished line across many chunks. This release bounds retained EventSource parser state, including field counts, buffered chunks, unfinished-line length, and retained field data.

... (truncated)

title: test-runner: splitQueries() mis-splits $$ heredocs and escaped backticks (8 upstream tests affected)
body:
Follow-up to #1074, which was closed after #1085 removed all SQL rewriting from the client. The one place this repository still scans SQL by hand is the upstream test harness in `tests/clickhouse-test-runner`:

- `src/split-queries.ts` splits a `.sql` test file into statements on `;`, tracking `'`, `"`, backticks, backslash escapes, `--` and `/* */` comments.
- `src/test-hint.ts` and `src/backends/rowbinary.ts` skip leading comments with the same two comment styles.

## Measurement

To find out how much this limits the allowlist, I compared `splitQueries()` with a split on the official lexer's `Semicolon` tokens ([`@clickhouse/lexer`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@clickhouse/lexer) 1.0.1) over every `tests/queries/0_stateless/*.sql` file in ClickHouse/ClickHouse at 3c82fa8c (2026-10-31).

| | files |
|---|---|
| compared | 13036 |
| identical split | 13010 |
| different split | 9 |
| official lexer reports an error token | 17 |

Of the 9 differences, 1 is allowlisted and benign (`01280_unicode_whitespaces_lexer`: only the decoded text of a U+FEFF character differs, the statement boundaries are the same). The other 8 are not allowlisted and are split wrong by the harness:

- **`$$ ... $$` heredocs** (7 files): the splitter does not know dollar quoting, so a `'` or `"` inside the heredoc toggles its quote state and the following statements are merged into one. `02683_native_too_large_size`, `02685_bson2`, `02686_bson3`, `02687_native_fuzz`, `03011_definitive_guide_to_cast` (82 statements found, 91 expected), `03032_save_bad_json_escape_sequences`, `04038_ascii_cjk_tokenizer` (28 found, 43 expected).
- **Backslash-escaped backtick in an identifier** (1 file): `04097_tuple_inside_nullable_subcolumn_descendants` (15 found, 18 expected).

The 17 files the official lexer rejects are KQL-dialect tests (`!`, `1.5h`), raw TSV inserts containing a lone `\`, a `#` that is not a comment (`03811_test_hint_after_comment`) and similar. The hand-written splitter handles them, so any lexer-based splitter would need a fallback.

Synthetic inputs also show the splitter mishandles `#`, `#!` and `//` line comments and nested block comments that contain a `;`, but no upstream test file hits those.

## Suggested scope

The numbers do not justify adopting the lexer in the harness: 8 candidate files out of about 10000 not yet allowlisted. The cheap fix is to teach `splitQueries()` dollar quoting (`$$...$$` and `$tag$...$tag$`) and backslash escapes inside backticks, with the affected upstream files as regression cases. Whether those 8 tests then pass through the harness for other reasons is a separate question.

title: fix(test-runner): split $$ heredocs and escaped backticks in splitQueries()
body:
Fixes #1096.

## Summary

`splitQueries()` in the upstream SQL test harness only tracked `'`, `"` and backticks, backslash escapes outside backticks, and the two comment styles. The server lexer also has dollar quoting and honors backslash escapes inside quoted identifiers, so two constructs were mis-split:

- **`$$ ... $$` / `$tag$ ... $tag$` heredocs** (7 upstream files). A `'` or `"` inside the heredoc toggled the splitter's quote state, so the remaining statements were merged into one, and a `;` inside the heredoc could split it. Example: `03011_definitive_guide_to_cast` was seen as 82 statements instead of 91, `04038_ascii_cjk_tokenizer` as 28 instead of 43.
- **A backslash-escaped backtick inside a quoted identifier** (1 upstream file). `` `a\`b` `` closed the identifier early, leaving it open and merging the rest of the file: `04097_tuple_inside_nullable_subcolumn_descendants` was seen as 15 statements instead of 18.

## Root Cause

`src/split-queries.ts` hand-scans the SQL with three quote flags and no notion of dollar quoting. It also only entered the escape handling for `'` and `"` (`if ((inSingleQuote || inDoubleQuote) && ch === "\\")`), while the server lexer's `quotedString<>()` treats `'`, `"` and `` ` `` identically. There is no bug in ClickHouse; this is purely the harness's statement splitter disagreeing with `src/Parsers/Lexer.cpp` about where a statement ends.

## Technical Solution

Kept the hand-written scanner (the issue's measurement does not justify adopting the lexer, and 17 upstream files use syntax the lexer rejects) and taught it the two missing rules, mirroring the lexer:

- `findHeredocEnd()` implements the lexer's `$` branch: an opening `$`, an optional tag of word characters (`[A-Za-z0-9_]`), and `$` again; the heredoc then extends to the next occurrence of the same delimiter. An unterminated delimiter is not a heredoc, and its `$` stays an ordinary character. The region is copied verbatim, so quotes, comment markers and semicolons inside it cannot affect the split.
- Backslash escapes are now recognized inside backticks as well, matching `quotedString<'`'>()`.

No parser rewrite, no new dependency, no change to `test-hint.ts` or the backends.

Resulting statement counts on the files named in the issue now match the official lexer: `03011` 82 -> 91, `04038` 28 -> 43, `04097` 15 -> 18, and `02683`/`02685`/`02686`/`02687`/`03032` split at the correct boundary. A 150-file sample of `tests/queries/0_stateless` produces byte-identical output before and after, so no currently allowlisted file changes behavior. Adding the affected tests to `upstream-allowlist.txt` is deliberately left out: per `tests/clickhouse-test-runner/AGENTS.md`, allowlist growth is validated separately through the harness against both CI server versions.

## Test Plan

New cases in `tests/clickhouse-test-runner/__tests__/split-queries.test.ts` (heredoc with quotes/backslashes, tagged heredoc, statement boundaries after a heredoc, unterminated `$$`, `$foo` not being a heredoc, escaped backtick in a quoted identifier). All four heredoc/backtick cases fail on `main` and pass with the fix.

Commands run locally (Node 24.22.1, Windows):

```
cd tests/clickhouse-test-runner
npx vitest run                 # 7 files, 86 tests passed
npx tsc --noEmit               # clean (after building packages/datatype-parser and the rowbinary skill)
npm run lint                   # eslint --max-warnings=0, clean
npx prettier --check src/split-queries.ts __tests__/split-queries.test.ts   # clean
```

Statement counts old vs new were compared by running both implementations over the upstream files from the issue plus a 150-file sample of `tests/queries/0_stateless` (ClickHouse master).

No changelog entry: `tests/clickhouse-test-runner` is a private, unpublished workspace package with no `CHANGELOG.md`, and no published package changes.

## Checklist

- [x] Unit tests covering the fixed behaviour were added
- [x] Changelog: not applicable (private test-harness package, no published API change)
- [ ] Docs: not applicable (internal harness behaviour)

title: fix(rowbinary): preserve duplicate Map keys with readMapEntries
body:
## Summary

`@clickhouse/rowbinary` folded the pairs of a `Map(K, V)` into a JS `Map`, so pairs sharing a key collapsed and only the last value survived, even though the wire carries every pair. This adds an opt-in pair-preserving reader (`readMapEntries`), keeps `readMap` returning a `Map`, and threads the same choice through the schema-driven readers.

Fixes #996

## Root Cause

ClickHouse `Map(K, V)` is not unique by key (the docs state a map can contain two elements with the same key), and RowBinary encodes it as a flattened `Array(Tuple(K, V))` with a LEB128 count. Every pair is therefore on the wire and is consumed by the reader. `readMap` then did `out.set(key, value)`: for a repeated key that overwrites the earlier value, so the pair was decoded and then discarded. `src/readers/compile.ts` and `src/readers/dynamic.ts` emit the same `Map.set` shape because they fold/parse into `readMap`.

## Fix

- New `readMapEntries(readKey, readValue): Reader<Array<[K, V]>>` in `src/readers/composite.ts`. It returns one entry per wire pair, in wire order, duplicates included.
- `readMap` is now a thin wrapper over it (`new Map(readMapEntries(...)(state))`), so the existing `Reader<Map<K, V>>` return type is unchanged and callers that do not need duplicates see no difference.
- New exported `ReadOptions { mapAsEntries?: boolean }` in `composite.ts`, wired into `astToReader` and `typeStringToReader` (`compile.ts`) and into `readDynamicType` / `readDynamic` (`dynamic.ts`). It is part of the recursion, so it applies at any depth: top-level map, map-in-array, map-in-map, inside `Tuple` / `Variant` / `Nested`, and a `Map` carried by a `Dynamic` value.
- Exports flow through the existing `src/readers/reader.ts` barrel (`export * from "./composite.js"`).

```ts
import { readMapEntries } from "@clickhouse/rowbinary";

// SELECT CAST(map('key', 'X', 'key', 'Y') AS Map(String, String)) FORMAT RowBinary
const read = readMapEntries(readString, readString);
read(cursor); // [["key", "X"], ["key", "Y"]]

// Schema-driven path:
const compiled = typeStringToReader("Map(String, String)", {
  mapAsEntries: true,
});
```

## Test Plan

New test file `skills/clickhouse-js-node-rowbinary/tests/MapEntries.test.ts` builds the duplicate-key payload by hand (no ClickHouse server needed, so it runs in CI and locally): `0x02` count, then `"key"/"X"` and `"key"/"Y"`, 13 bytes, matching what `SELECT CAST(map('key','X','key','Y') AS Map(String,String)) FORMAT RowBinary` returns. It covers `readMapEntries` at top level and on the empty map, `readMap` on the same bytes (still `Map(1) { 'key' => 'Y' }`, i.e. unchanged API) and on unique keys, plus the option working for a top-level map, a map in an `Array`, a map in a `Map` value, a map inside a `Dynamic` value, and the default (no option) shape.

Commands run from the repository root unless noted, all locally on Windows with Node.js 24:

- `cd skills/clickhouse-js-node-rowbinary && npm ci` : installed, exit 0.
- `cd skills/clickhouse-js-node-rowbinary && npx vitest run tests/MapEntries.test.ts` : `Test Files 1 passed (1)`, `Tests 9 passed (9)`.
- `cd skills/clickhouse-js-node-rowbinary && npx tsc --noEmit` : exit 0, no type errors.
- `npx prettier --check skills/clickhouse-js-node-rowbinary/src/readers/{composite,compile,dynamic,rowBinaryWithNamesAndTypes}.ts skills/clickhouse-js-node-rowbinary/tests/MapEntries.test.ts` : `All matched files use Prettier code style!`

The pre-existing reader tests in this package (`tests/Map.test.ts`, `tests/compile.test.ts`, framing tests, ...) query a live ClickHouse server, so they were left to CI; `tsc` covers their unchanged call sites. No full suite was run locally.

## Checklist

- [x] Unit test covering the regression was added (`tests/MapEntries.test.ts`, server-free)
- [x] A human-readable changelog entry was added to `skills/clickhouse-js-node-rowbinary/CHANGELOG.md`
- [ ] Documentation update in clickhouse-docs (not needed: this is an opt-in addition inside the package, with no docs page describing `readMap` today)

title: fix: keep oversized multipart parts out of the form body
body:
## Summary

Fixes #1089. `use_multipart_params` / `use_multipart_params_auto` could not handle any value larger than the server's form field cap: a large SQL statement was rejected only because multipart mode moved it into the `query` part, and an oversized parameter was promoted out of the URL only to be rejected by the form parser. Both failed with `Poco::Exception ... HTML Form Exception: Field value too long`.

## Root cause

ClickHouse parses a `multipart/form-data` body with Poco's `HTMLForm` before the query's own `clickhouse_settings` are applied, and caps every individual field value at `http_max_field_value_size` (128 KiB by default). The multipart path put both the statement and each `param_*` value into form fields, so the cap applied to values that travel outside a form otherwise:

- the SQL statement is normally the raw request body, bounded only by `max_query_size`;
- with `use_multipart_params_auto`, a parameter over 128 KiB was moved out of the URL (avoiding HTTP 414) and into a form field that is equally unable to carry it.

Passing `http_max_field_value_size` in `clickhouse_settings` does not help, because the body is parsed before those settings take effect.

## Changes

- `packages/client-common`: adds `MAX_FORM_FIELD_VALUE_LENGTH` (128 KiB, the default `http_max_field_value_size`) and `exceedsMultipartFieldLimit()`, which compares the UTF-8 byte length, and documents the cap and the fallback on both options in `config.ts`.
- `packages/client-node` and `packages/client-web`: the multipart parts are now assembled once, before the transport decision. If the statement or any parameter exceeds the form field budget, the request falls back to the non-multipart layout - the statement is sent as the raw body and the parameters stay in the URL. That is exactly how the same request behaves without multipart, so the oversized value no longer depends on a form parser that is guaranteed to reject it. A parameter at the limit still goes into the form.

The fallback is per request; a multipart request whose parts fit keeps using the form body.

## Test plan

Server-free regression tests:

- `packages/client-common/__tests__/unit/multipart.test.ts` - at the limit, one byte over, and multi-byte UTF-8 measurement: 19 passed.
- `packages/client-node/__tests__/unit/node_multipart_query.test.ts` - oversized statement, oversized param in explicit and auto mode, and a param exactly at the limit (still multipart): 15 passed. The node HTTP stub does not exercise the piped body, so the raw-body assertion lives in the web spec.
- `packages/client-web/__tests__/unit/web_multipart_query.test.ts` - the same four cases plus `init.body === query` for the fallback: 15 passed. The suite runs in Playwright here; the sandbox could not bind the browser server, so I ran this file against its sources with a scratch Node-environment config outside the repo. CI runs it in the browser as usual.
- `packages/client-common/__tests__/integration/multipart_params.test.ts` - both reproductions from the issue (200 KB statement, 200 KB parameter in auto mode) now expect a successful result. Not run locally: no ClickHouse image was available and the repo directs integration coverage to CI.

Also run: `tsc --noEmit` in all three packages (exit 0), `eslint --max-warnings=0` for client-node and client-web (clean), Prettier on all changed files (clean).

## Checklist

- [x] Unit and integration tests covering the common scenarios were added
- [x] A human-readable changelog entry was added to every affected package's `CHANGELOG.md` (`packages/client-node/CHANGELOG.md` and `packages/client-web/CHANGELOG.md`)
- [ ] For significant changes, documentation in https://github.com/ClickHouse/clickhouse-docs was updated with further explanations or tutorials

title: fix: end the stream span once and keep its error on a query() format mismatch
body:
## Summary

Addresses the two Copilot findings on the 1.25.0 release PR #1102 ([span ended twice](https://github.com/ClickHouse/clickhouse-js/pull/1102#discussion_r4441969402), [unhandled rejection on Web](https://github.com/ClickHouse/clickhouse-js/pull/1102#discussion_r4441969327)). Both confirmed against the code; the second also reproduced directly (`ReadableStream.cancel()` rejects on an errored or locked stream).

When `query()` detects that the server answered in a different format than requested, it closes the `ResultSet` and throws. The `ResultSet` owns the `clickhouse.query.stream` span and ends it from `close()`, so the surrounding `catch` ended it a second time:

- **Node.js:** `close()` is synchronous, so the span was ended *before* the error was recorded on it — OpenTelemetry drops updates to an ended span, so the mismatch was lost from the trace. Custom tracers saw two `end()` calls, breaking the exactly-once contract in `tracing.ts`.
- **Web:** `close()` is async, so the order flipped but the span was still ended twice. And if cancelling the response stream rejected (e.g. connection reset right after the headers), that rejection was unhandled, and the Web `ResultSet` never ended its span at all.

## Changes

- `client.ts`: build the mismatch error, record it on the stream span, *then* close; wrap `close()` in `Promise.resolve(...).catch(() => {})` so a cleanup failure never surfaces next to the error the caller receives; the `catch` block only touches the span when no `ResultSet` was created (`spanOwnedByResultSet`).
- `client-web/result_set.ts`: `close()` finishes the span (with the cancel error) when `cancel()` rejects, instead of leaking it.
- Tests with a counting tracer for both clients: span ended exactly once, mismatch recorded, ERROR status; on Web additionally the errored-stream case (vitest fails the run on an unhandled rejection, so the test would catch a regression).

## Changelog

The `client.ts` part corrects behaviour new in the unreleased 1.25.0 (#1085), so no entry. The Web `close()` span leak exists in the released `client-web` 1.24.0, so it gets a "(Web only)" entry under `packages/client-web/CHANGELOG.md` → `# 1.25.0` (follow-up commit on this PR).

## Verification

- `typecheck`, `lint` (`--max-warnings=0`) and `prettier --check` pass for all three packages.
- Unit suites: client-node 421 passed, client-web 267 passed (incl. the new file). Two `client-common` unit tests fail locally, identically with this change stashed (`tracing.test.ts` error-code assertion and `client.test.ts` needing `environmentSpecificCreateClient`) — pre-existing / environment, not touched here.

See also the attributes-handling utilities provided by @opentelemetry/core to help. For example, cleanSimpleAttributes() can be used to limit user-provided attributes to the set of value types supported in earlier @opentelemetry/api versions.

v8.12.2

Security fixes

High severity

Denial of service via TLS 1.2 certificate-changing renegotiation

CVE-2026-87018 · GHSA-qrxm-fqhp-jwvm

A malicious or compromised HTTPS server could crash the Node.js process by initiating TLS 1.2 renegotiation and presenting a different, CA-trusted certificate whose hostname did not match the requested host. The resulting socket error reached an assertion in undici's HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 connection handling. This release handles post-connect certificate errors without terminating the process.

TLS certificate validation bypass through dropped Agent options

CVE-2026-109383 · GHSA-2m5v-pch6-74hx

Agent used a JSON-based clone for constructor options, which silently removed function-valued TLS options such as checkServerIdentity. Applications relying on custom certificate or public-key verification could therefore accept a certificate that the callback was intended to reject. This release preserves TLS options when creating per-origin dispatchers.

Cache poisoning and cross-user disclosure through cross-origin redirects

CVE-2026-109829 · GHSA-4w7w-5xrc-9h26

When an originless Agent combined redirect and shared-cache interceptors as compose(redirect(), cache()), a response from a cross-origin redirect could be stored under the original URL. This could allow persistent cache poisoning or disclosure of user-specific responses to later callers. This release verifies the response origin before caching and preserves redirect-hop cache-control policy.

Denial of service through excessive Content-Encoding values

CVE-2026-109869 · GHSA-xjj6-f33q-929c

A malicious HTTP server could crash the Node.js process by returning more than five content codings and closing the connection before sending the body. Although fetch() rejected the response, an error from an orphaned internal stream could remain unhandled. This release validates the content-encoding chain before creating the body stream and aborts oversized chains safely.

Medium severity

Denial of service through the decompress interceptor

CVE-2026-87029 · GHSA-55wc-3pg8-jfw6

title: test(upstream-sql-tests): run the 26.10 tests against the 26.10 server
body:
> [!NOTE]
> **Merge after `@clickhouse/client` 1.25.0 is published to `latest`.** This PR changes only the test runner and its workflow, so it can't affect the release. We're holding it so `main` doesn't change during the release.

## Summary

`upstream-sql-tests` has failed every night since 2026-10-25, and it is also the only red check on the 1.25.0 release PR (#1102, see [this comment](https://github.com/ClickHouse/clickhouse-js/pull/1102#issuecomment-6578285278)). This PR makes it pass again. With these changes, all 20 jobs pass against server 26.10.3.7 ([run 41451523273](https://github.com/ClickHouse/clickhouse-js/actions/runs/41451523273)).

**Cause.** The workflow runs ClickHouse's own SQL test suite against the `latest` server image, with the test suite pinned to a June 2026 ClickHouse commit. On 2026-10-25, `latest` moved from 26.9 to 26.10. 16 tests began to fail because the server output no longer matched the old expected results (for example, the byte layout of serialized aggregate states). On the same commit `e829009`, the workflow passed on 10-24 (server 26.9.19.9) and failed on 10-25 (server 26.10.2.103).

**Not a client regression.** With the suite pinned to 26.10, the same 9 tests fail on `release`, which is the 1.24.1 code ([run](https://github.com/ClickHouse/clickhouse-js/actions/runs/41446398353)), and on `main`, which is 1.25.0 ([run](https://github.com/ClickHouse/clickhouse-js/actions/runs/41445264743)). No test fails only on `main`.

## Changes

- **Pin the test suite to `v26.10.2.103-stable`**, the release that matches the `latest` server image.
- **Fix how the test runner behaves where it differed from `clickhouse-client`.** The test runner is our stand-in for `clickhouse-client`. These fixes bring back 7 of the 9 failing tests instead of dropping them:
  - **`--port`:** in `clickhouse-client`, `--port` is the native TCP port. Since the June version, the upstream runner exports `CLICKHOUSE_PORT_TCP`, and `shell_config.sh` adds `--port=9000` to `$CLICKHOUSE_CLIENT` for `.sh` tests. The test runner treated that as an HTTP port and sent HTTP to 9000. It now maps the native port to the HTTP port the runner exports. Any other port is still used as an HTTP port.
  - **`-n` and multiple statements:** in `clickhouse-client`, `-n` means `--multiquery` (`-m` means `--multiline`), and `-q` runs every statement whether or not `-n` is given. The test runner treated `-n` as `--multiline` and ignored it, and it only split statements when `--multiquery` was passed. `.sql` tests aren't affected, because the upstream runner always passes `--multiquery` for them. None of the 9 allowlisted `.sh` tests contains a `serverError` hint, so splitting their queries can't hide an error.
  - **Rowbinary Decimal output:** the rowbinary renderer printed Decimals with their full scale (`1.20`). The server's text output drops trailing zeros by default (`output_format_decimal_trailing_zeros = 0`) and prints `1.2`. The upstream runner never randomizes this setting.
- **Comment out three tests in the allowlist, with the reason inline:**
  - `03707_autopr_unsupported_cases` needs a `parallel_replicas` cluster in the server config.
  - `04103_plain_rewritable_get_last_modified_bug` needs `custom_local_disks_base_directory` in the server config.
  - `02515_generate_ulid` is blocked by a bug in the client's `parseError`. The server repeats the failing query inside its error message, and the regex takes the first all-caps word in parentheses as the error type. For this test's query, the type comes out as `NULL` instead of `TOO_MANY_ARGUMENTS_FOR_FUNCTION`, and the message is cut short at the same point. 1.24.1 behaves the same, so this isn't a regression. The fix will come in a separate PR with changelog entries for both clients, and that PR will re-enable this test.
- **Docs:** the README's CI section said `upstream_ref` defaults to `master` and that the matrix runs a `head` server column. Neither is true. It now explains the pin, and it describes the `--port` and multi-statement behaviour. The test runner's `AGENTS.md` has a note on what to do when `latest` moves to a new server release.

No changelog entry: the test runner isn't a published package.

## Test plan

- Workflow dispatched on this branch with the new pin: 20/20 jobs green ([run 41451523273](https://github.com/ClickHouse/clickhouse-js/actions/runs/41451523273)). The last commit only changes docs.
- Test runner unit tests: 84 passed, including new cases for `resolveHttpPort`, for `-n` / `-m`, and for Decimal trailing zeros. `tsc` and `eslint --max-warnings=0` pass.
- Smoke test against a local server: `-q "SELECT 1; SELECT 2;"` runs both statements, and `--port 9000 -n` reaches the server over HTTP.

Related: #1096 / #1097, which fix heredoc splitting in `split-queries.ts`. They cover different tests and don't touch the same files.

title: docs: changelog entry for the JSON-wrapped error message fix in 1.25.0
body:
## Summary

Adds a missing changelog entry for #1085 to the `# 1.25.0` sections of both client changelogs. Merge it **before** the `@clickhouse/client-web` 1.25.0 release PR, so the Web release notes include it.

Besides the `default_format` change, #1085 also changed `parseError()`. When the server reports an error in a JSON output format, `parseError()` now unwraps it, so `ClickHouseError.message` no longer keeps the JSON escaping. Neither changelog mentioned this.

**Checked against 26.11.1.312, with `max_block_size=1` and a `throwIf()` partway through a `JSONEachRow` result:**

| `http_write_exception_in_output_format` | Error shape (1.24.0 and 1.25.0 requests alike) | 1.24.0 `message` | 1.25.0 `message` |
|---|---|---|---|
| `0` (26.11 default) | plain `__exception__` block | `bad "quoted" value` | `bad "quoted" value` |
| `1` | `{"exception": "..."}` | `bad \"quoted\" value` | `bad "quoted" value` |

So the improvement shows only with that setting enabled, and the entry says so. #1085 also says that 24.8 now returns pre-execution errors as JSON because the format is sent as a setting. On 24.8 the new unwrapping keeps the message the same as before, so that part needs no entry.

## `@clickhouse/client` (Node.js)

1.25.0 is already released, so this adds the line to a released section. Once this PR is merged, I'll update the [client-1.25.0 GitHub Release](https://github.com/ClickHouse/clickhouse-js/releases/tag/client-1.25.0) to match. npm doesn't need any change.

title: Release process: only build head for the package being released, and publish latest from the tested commit
body:
## Problem

The client publish workflows decide whether to start a `head` (pre-release) build from **which files changed in a push to `release`**. They don't check **which package is being released**. `release` is shared by all packages, and both clients bundle `packages/client-common/**` and depend on the root `package-lock.json`. So a release of one client usually starts a `head` run for the other client as well. Each of those runs stops at the `npm-publish` approval gate, and someone has to reject or cancel it.

This happened in both 1.25.0 releases:

- **`@clickhouse/client` 1.25.0** (#1102): the shared code changed, so `publish-client-web.yml` started a Web `head` run ([41454358459](https://github.com/ClickHouse/clickhouse-js/actions/runs/41454358459)), which had to be cancelled. If it had been approved, it would have published `1.24.0-head.bfd729c.1`: a pre-release of 1.24.0 with post-1.24.0 code in it, which sorts **before** the released 1.24.0.
- **`@clickhouse/client-web` 1.25.0** (#1110): the version bump changed `package-lock.json`, and #1109 changed `packages/client-node/CHANGELOG.md`, so `publish-client.yml` started a Node `head` run ([41858720860](https://github.com/ClickHouse/clickhouse-js/actions/runs/41858720860)). It would have published `1.25.0-head.a5b9c61.1`, a pre-release of the already released 1.25.0. Cancelling it from the UI, cancelling and force-cancelling it through the API, and rejecting it through the API all failed, and the run is still stuck at the gate.
- **A mislabelled build is already on npm.** `@clickhouse/client-web@head` is `1.24.0-head.6a265d2.1`. It was published on 2026-10-09 during the Node-only 1.24.1 release, so it's post-1.24.0 code labelled as a 1.24.0 pre-release.

Two related points about the current process:
- `head` and `latest` are **separate builds**; nothing is promoted. The `latest` dispatch builds again from whatever `release` points to when it starts. If anything merges into `release` between testing the `head` build and starting `latest`, `latest` ships untested code, and nothing prevents that.
- Releasing both clients together is often right, because shared code changes affect both. Today that takes two version bumps, two release PRs and two rounds of approvals, and we usually only realise it's needed partway through.

## Proposal

### 1. Build `head` only for a package with an unreleased version

In each client workflow, add a job without an environment, ahead of the gated `head` job. It checks whether the version in that package's `package.json` is already on npm:

```yaml
plan:                       # no environment, so no approval request
  if: github.event_name == 'push'
  runs-on: ubuntu-latest
  outputs:
    publish: ${{ steps.check.outputs.publish }}
  steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@…
    - id: check
      run: |
        v=$(node -p "require('./packages/client-web/package.json').version")
        if npm view "@clickhouse/client-web@$v" version >/dev/null 2>&1; then
          echo "publish=false" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"   # already released: no pre-release
        else
          echo "publish=true"  >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
        fi

publish-head:
  needs: plan
  if: needs.plan.outputs.publish == 'true'
  environment: npm-publish  # applies only when the job runs
```

- A skipped job never reaches the environment, so **no approval request is created and nothing has to be cancelled**.
- **The version bump becomes the signal to release.** Bump one client and only that client gets a `head` build. Bump both and both do.
- **No more mislabelled versions:** a `head` build only exists for a version that hasn't shipped.
- **Fixing forward still works.** If a `head` build is bad, fix it on `main` and sync `release` again: the version is still unreleased, so a new `head` build is published. (A check like "did the version change in this push?" would lose this.)
- The existing `paths:` filters stay as a cheap first filter.

This is much smaller than #695, which compared tarball contents and was closed as too complex. It fixes a different problem: unwanted runs and wrong versions, not no-op churn.

### 2. Make `latest` publish the commit that was tested

The `latest` dispatch takes the tested `head` version, or its commit, as an input, and refuses to start if `release` no longer points to that commit. npm versions can't be renamed, so this isn't promotion, but it guarantees that `latest` is built from the code that was tested.

### 3. Bump both clients in one PR when shared code changed

`bump-version.yml` accepts several packages, for example `@clickhouse/client,@clickhouse/client-web`, and opens a single PR. The release skill checks for `client-common` changes since each client's last release tag and asks up front whether to release both. With item 1, that means one bump PR, one release PR, and only the `head` builds you want.

### 4. Housekeeping

- Move `@clickhouse/client-web`'s `head` tag off `1.24.0-head.6a265d2.1`.
- Update `.claude/skills/release/SKILL.md`:
  - `head` and `latest` are separate builds;
  - which `head` runs start and why;
  - only the `npm-publish` required reviewers can approve a publish;
  - `gh run watch` exits early on a run paused at an approval gate, so poll until the run completes instead.

## Suggested order

Items 1 and 2 in one PR to `publish-client.yml` and `publish-client-web.yml`, plus the skill notes from item 4. Item 3 afterwards.

Not in scope: loosening the `npm-publish` approval for `head` builds. With item 1, the approvals that remain are all for builds someone wants, and removing the gate is a security decision.

title: fix(types): export the remaining public API types from #998
body:
## Summary

This PR exports four more types from `@clickhouse/client` and `@clickhouse/client-web`. The public API uses them:

| Type | Where the public API uses it |
| --- | --- |
| `ResultStream` | Return type of `ResultSet.stream()` |
| `WithResponseHeaders` | Part of `CommandResult` and `ExecResult` |
| `PingParamsWithEndpoint` | Member of the `PingParams` union |
| `PingParamsWithSelectQuery` | Member of the `PingParams` union. The `ping()` JSDoc links to it. |

#1024 exported the six types from #997. @Saitgalin found these four as well in #998. The fork of #998 is archived, so this PR carries over the part of #998 that #1024 does not cover. The commit has a `Co-authored-by` trailer for the original author, and both changelogs thank them.

The change is type-only. There is no runtime change.

## Team feedback requested

These exports are not strictly necessary. Users can get each type from types that are already exported:

- `Extract<PingParams, { select: true }>` / `Extract<PingParams, { select: false }>`
- `{ response_headers: ResponseHeaders }`
- `ReturnType<ResultSet<F>['stream']>`. This is awkward, because `stream<T>()` is generic and `T` becomes `unknown`.

Each export is a permanent API commitment. For the ping types, it makes the structure of the `PingParams` union public. `ResultStream` has the best use case (generic helpers over `Format`). Please tell us if we must keep all four, only `ResultStream`, or none.

## Checklist

- [x] Changelogs updated (`client-node`, `client-web`, new `1.25.1` heading)
- [x] `npm run typecheck`, eslint, prettier pass

title: ci: fix dependency installs on the ubuntu-26.04 runner image
body:
## Problem

All CI jobs now fail in the `Install dependencies` step, before any test starts. #1119 is an example.

- Our workflows use `runs-on: ubuntu-latest`. On 2026-11-09, `ubuntu-latest` changed from `ubuntu-24.04` to `ubuntu-26.04`. The `node` run on `main` at 09:16 used 24.04. The run on #1119 at 11:36 used 26.04, on the same base commit.
- `ubuntu-26.04` has GCC 15. The native addon of `simdjson@0.9.2` does not compile with GCC 15:

  ```
  error: inlining failed in call to 'always_inline' '__m128i _mm_clmulepi64_si128(...)': target specific option mismatch
  gyp ERR! cwd .../node_modules/simdjson
  ```

- `simdjson` has had no release since 2022, so a fix from upstream is unlikely.

The next run on `main` will also fail.

## Change

`simdjson` was a dev dependency of `packages/client-node`. Only two tests used it, as an example custom `parse` function:

- `__tests__/unit/node_values_encoder.test.ts`: The custom encoder now uses a wrapper around `JSON.parse`.
- `__tests__/integration/node_stream_json_each_row_with_progress.test.ts`: The test "should work with simdjson parser" did the same insert and query as "should use custom parse when querying with JSONEachRow". The result check moves to that test, and the duplicate test is removed. Coverage stays the same.

The lockfile change only removes `simdjson` and `node-addon-api` (21 lines). `node-addon-api` had no other users.

This change affects only dev dependencies and tests, so the published packages do not change. No changelog entry.

### Second problem: Playwright in `examples/web`

After the first fix, both `run-examples (web)` jobs failed:

```
Error: ERROR: Playwright does not support chromium on ubuntu26.04-x64
```

`examples/web` used Playwright 1.60.0. This PR changes it to 1.64.1, the same version that the root workspace uses. The browser test jobs (`chromium` / `firefox`) already pass on `ubuntu-26.04` with 1.64.1. Version 1.64.1 was released on 2026-10-14, so it passes the 7-day age audit. The lockfile change has only the Playwright entries.

## Verification

- `npm ci --ignore-scripts --dry-run` accepts the lockfile.
- `npm run typecheck` and prettier pass.
- `node_values_encoder.test.ts`: 13 passed.
- `node_stream_json_each_row_with_progress.test.ts` against a local ClickHouse server: 8 passed.

## Note

title: chore(deps): group Dependabot updates into one weekly PR per ecosystem
body:
## Summary

Separate Dependabot PRs each change `package-lock.json`. When we merge one PR, the other PRs get merge conflicts. This change puts the updates into one PR for each ecosystem.

- **npm:** one weekly PR for all npm updates (`patterns: ["*"]`). This group replaces the `vitest` and `dev-dependencies` groups. The Vitest packages are still in the same group, so they still move together.
- **GitHub Actions:** one weekly PR for all action updates (`patterns: ["*"]`). This group replaces the `workflows` group, which took only development-type dependencies.

## No change

- The schedule (weekly, Monday).
- The 7-day cooldown and the `@clickhouse/*` exclusion.
- The `ignore` rules.
- Security updates. The groups do not set `applies-to`, so they apply to version updates only. Security updates still open as separate PRs immediately, and the cooldown does not apply to them.

## Checklist

- No CHANGELOG entry: this change is CI configuration only, with no effect on the packages.

title: docs: fix URL parameter name application_id -> application
body:
## Summary
The URL configuration table in `docs/clickhouse-docs/index.mdx` listed `application_id`. The URL parser has only ever accepted `application`, which is also the name of the config option. This PR changes the docs to match the code.

## Background
- The `application` URL parameter was added in #232 (`loadConfigOptionsFromURL` in `packages/client-common/src/config.ts`). Since then the parser has accepted `?application=` and rejected `?application_id=` with `Unknown URL parameters`.
- The docs text above the table already says a URL parameter's name "reflects its path in the config options interface", and the config option is `application`.
- `application_id` exists only as the internal `ConnectionParams` field. `getConnectionParams` fills it from `config.application`. A code scan finds no other place that reads it from a URL.

We're fixing the docs instead of adding an `application_id` alias (#1088) so the public API doesn't get a second, permanent name for the same option.

Docs-only, so there's no behaviour change and no changelog entry.

Fixes #1052

title: ci!: drop Node.js 20 (end of life 2026-04-30)
body:
## Summary

Node.js 20 reached [end of life](https://endoflife.date/nodejs) on 2026-04-30. The client documentation says that the client supports all the [maintained](https://github.com/nodejs/release#readme) Node.js releases, and drops a version when it approaches end of life. This PR applies that policy. It follows the same pattern as the Node.js 18 drop in #906.

Maintained Node.js releases today: 22.x (EOL 2027-04-30), 24.x and 26.x.

### CI
- Removed `20` from every Node.js matrix: `tests-node` (×3), `tests-cloud`, `tests-oss-dependents`, `tests-skill-rowbinary`, `publish-client`, `publish-datatype-parser`, `publish-skill-rowbinary`. They are now `[22, 24, 26]`.

### `engines.node`
- `@clickhouse/client`, `@clickhouse/datatype-parser`, `@clickhouse/rowbinary`, `examples/node`, `examples/web`: `>=20` → `>=22`.
- Root `package.json` and `tests/clickhouse-test-runner`: `>=20.19.0` → `>=22.13.0`. This matches the dev tooling: ESLint 10 needs `^22.13.0` and Vite 8 needs `>=22.12.0` on the 22 line.
- Matching updates in the lockfiles (workspace and example root entries only; no transitive dependencies changed).
- `@clickhouse/client-web` and `@clickhouse/client-common` have no `engines` field, so they do not change.

### Documentation
- `README.md`, `packages/client-node/README.md`: removed the `20.x` row.
- `docs/clickhouse-docs/index.mdx`: this table was out of date. It had no `26.x` row and still showed `18.x` as "Best effort". It now matches the README (26, 24, 22).
- `CONTRIBUTING.md`, `examples/README.md`, `demo/logs/README.md`: updated the Node.js versions.
- Agent skills: `setup`, `release` and `typescript-lsp` (`.claude/skills/`), and `clickhouse-js-node-coding/reference/custom-json.md`. The `JSON.parse` reviver `context.source` is available on every supported Node.js version now, so the recipe no longer lists a 20.x requirement.
- Code comments: `tests/e2e/install/src/integration.ts` (the "no TS-only syntax" rule still applies, because Node 22 before 22.18.0 does not strip types by default) and `packages/datatype-parser/src/json.ts`.

### Changelogs
- `@clickhouse/client`: Migration Notes entry. The unreleased top heading `1.25.1` was renamed to `1.26.0`, because dropping a runtime is more than a patch (the Node.js 18 drop shipped in the minor release 1.23.0).
- `@clickhouse/datatype-parser`: new `0.1.4` heading (patch, as in #906 for 0.1.3). A `0.2.0` would fall outside the `^0.1.2` range that `@clickhouse/rowbinary` uses.
- `@clickhouse/rowbinary`: new `0.2.1` heading.
- `@clickhouse/client-web`: no entry, because this change does not affect the Web package.

### Not changed
- `packages/client-node/__tests__/tls/tls.test.ts:92` has a `FIXME` that says error-message matching "does not work on Node.js 18/20". It may work on 22+ now, but this PR does not verify that.
- The zstd runtime check (Node.js >= 22.15.0) stays, because the new floor is `>=22`.

## Security and API impact
- No security or data-privacy impact. No code paths change.
- User-facing: an install of `@clickhouse/client`, `@clickhouse/datatype-parser` or `@clickhouse/rowbinary` on Node.js 20 now emits an `EBADENGINE` warning. The public API does not change.

## Checklist

- [x] A human-readable changelog entry was added to every affected package's `CHANGELOG.md`
- [ ] For significant changes, documentation in https://github.com/ClickHouse/clickhouse-docs was updated (`docs/clickhouse-docs/index.mdx` is the embedded copy. The `docs_sync` workflow copies it to ClickHouse/ClickHouse on a release, or at merge if this PR has the `sync-docs` label)

> **Overview**
> This PR **ends official support for Node.js 20** now that it has reached end of life, mirroring the earlier Node 18 drop. Supported runtimes are **22.x, 24.x, and 26.x** only.

feat(node): add an optional undici transport
body:
## Summary

Adds an **optional, opt-in undici transport** for the Node.js client. The default transport (`node:http` / `node:https`) does not change.

```ts
import { createClient } from "@clickhouse/client";
import { undiciTransport } from "@clickhouse/client/undici";

const client = createClient({ transport: undiciTransport() });
```

Refs #511. This PR is stacked on #1124 (Node.js 20 removed), because undici 8 needs Node.js ≥22.19.0.

### Goal

The goal is **less custom connection code and fewer bugs**, not speed. Most of `socket_pool.ts` exists because `node:http` does not give us keep-alive handling, timeouts and abort handling that we can trust. undici gives us these natively:
- keep-alive that uses the server `Keep-Alive: timeout=N` hint;
- a check of an idle socket before it is used again (the #294 case);
- `headersTimeout` / `bodyTimeout`;
- native `AbortSignal` support.

About speed: the latency difference in #779 does not come from `node:http`. It comes from `await sleep(0)` in `SocketPool.request()`, which adds about 2 ms to each request. Without that line, `node:http` and undici are about equally fast. `fetch()` on Node.js downloads about 10× slower (WebStreams), so it is not an option for this client.

## Design rules

1. **The `node:http` transport does not change.** The code is moved where necessary, but its behavior is the same, including its known bugs (see "Known `node:http` bugs" below).
2. **undici does its work natively.** Custom code is only for a real undici issue (see "Workarounds for undici").
3. **The API does not depend on the transport.** The undici transport gives the same errors as the `node:http` transport. Transport-independent error types for v2: #1129.

## Changes

### Transport interface

- `connection/transport.ts`: the internal `NodeTransport` interface (`request()`, `close()`) and the public, experimental `TransportFactory` type. `SocketPool` implements `NodeTransport`.
- `connection/response.ts`: the response handling that does not depend on the transport, moved out of `SocketPool`: decompression, the error-response check and `parseError`, and the summary. Both transports use it.
- The TLS auth headers (`X-ClickHouse-User` / `-Key` / `-SSL-Certificate-Auth`) moved from `NodeHttpsConnection` to the base connection, so that they apply to every transport.
- `NodeTransportConnection`: the connection class for a plugged-in transport. `transport` together with `http_agent` throws a clear error.

### Abort handling

- The abort-signal wrapper (`getAbortController()`) moved from `NodeBaseConnection` to the three `node:http` connection classes, through the new `getRequestAbort()` hook (`connection/request_abort.ts`). The base class calls the hook at the same points as before, so the `node:http` behavior is the same.
- The default of the hook passes the user's `abort_signal` unchanged. The undici transport gives it to undici, with no custom abort code.

| Case | `node:http` (unchanged) | undici |
|---|---|---|
| `abort_signal` already aborted | the request is sent (#1047) | `AbortError`, the request is not sent |
| Abort while the response body streams | ignored; the stream stops only at `request_timeout`, or never | the stream stops at once |

### Errors

`undici/errors.ts` maps the undici errors to the `node:http` errors (message and code), with the undici error in `cause`. I compared 12 failure cases with both transports; 11 give the same error.

| Failure | Both transports |
|---|---|
| Closed before the response headers | `socket hang up` (`ECONNRESET`) |
| Closed, reset, timeout or abort while the body streams | `aborted` (`ECONNRESET`) |
| Response headers too large | `Parse Error: Header overflow` (`HPE_HEADER_OVERFLOW`) |
| Invalid response | `Parse Error: <reason>`; **no `HPE_*` code with undici** |
| No response headers within `request_timeout` | `Timeout error.` |
| User abort | `name: "AbortError"`, `The user aborted a request.` |
| `ECONNREFUSED`, `ENOTFOUND`, a reset before the headers | unchanged (from `node:net`) |

### Option mapping

| Client option | undici `Agent` option |
|---|---|
| `max_open_connections` | `connections` (`Infinity` → `null`) |
| `request_timeout` | `headersTimeout` + `bodyTimeout` |
| `keep_alive.enabled: false` | `pipelining: 0` |
| `keep_alive.idle_socket_ttl` | `keepAliveTimeout` + `keepAliveMaxTimeout` |
| `tls` | `connect: { ca, cert, key }` |
| `max_response_headers_size` | `maxHeaderSize` |
| `request_timeout` | `connectTimeout` (else undici uses 10 s) |
| — | `allowH2: false` (undici 8 negotiates HTTP/2 by default; behind an h2 proxy, the connection limits stop working, and a cut-off response can look complete) |

`undiciTransport({ agent_options })` overrides these values.

### Optional dependency and entry point

- `undici` is **not** in the manifest, also not as an optional peer dependency: npm checks an optional peer dependency that is installed, so an application that depends on undici 6 or 7 got `ERESOLVE` on install, also without this transport. `undiciTransport()` checks the installed version at runtime instead: 8.12.3 or a later 8.x version, else a clear error. `dependencies` stays empty.
- Only the new `@clickhouse/client/undici` entry point imports undici. The main entry point does not (checked with `require.cache`), so bundlers and TypeScript users without undici are not affected.
- The entry point is a `undici/package.json` folder stub, not an `exports` field, because an `exports` field would block the deep imports that work today.
- Native ESM does not resolve a directory (`ERR_UNSUPPORTED_DIR_IMPORT`), so the folder has a real `undici/index.js`, and native ESM imports **`@clickhouse/client/undici/index.js`**. CommonJS, TypeScript (`nodenext`, `bundler`, `node10`) and bundlers accept both paths. An `exports` field waits for v2 (#1129), because it breaks extensionless deep imports such as `@clickhouse/client/dist/config`.
- `.scripts/smoke_test_pack.sh` checks the packed tarball: the main entry point without undici installed, then the undici entry point from ESM and CommonJS. The `dist` workflow now runs it on PRs.

## Workarounds for undici

| undici behavior | Workaround |
|---|---|
| `BodyReadable` emits `RequestAbortedError` when you call `destroy()` on a body that you have not read to the end. When the request is already complete, undici adds no `error` listener, so this is an **uncaught exception** (found by `default_format_constraint.test.ts` in CI) | `destroy()` without an error does not emit this error (the `node:http` behavior). The request is still aborted, and the connection is released |
| `bodyTimeout` does not run while the body is paused, so a result that the application does not read holds its connection forever. With all `max_open_connections` in use, the client hangs (found by @joe-clickhouse against a real server) | An idle timer on the body, restarted by each chunk that undici pushes, destroys it after `request_timeout`: the same as an idle socket with `node:http` |
| An abort of a request that waits for a connection only stores the reason; the request rejects when it gets a connection, which can be never | Reject at once when the signal aborts; undici then does not send the request |
| Bun replaces the `undici` module, and its `Agent` has no `request()` | A clear error at client creation. The docs say that the undici transport does not work on Bun |
| `HTTPParserError.code` is always `undefined` in undici 8 (it reads its llhttp error table by number, but the table maps names to numbers) | None: the message is mapped, the `code` is missing. Not reported upstream yet |

## Tests

- `CLICKHOUSE_TEST_TRANSPORT=undici` (in `vitest.setup.ts`) runs the test suite with the undici transport. Test clients that set their own `http_agent`, `transport` or `connection` keep them. The TLS tests also go through this switch.
- CI (cloud): `tests-cloud.yml` has one undici job (Node 24). The cloud service is shared and has limits, so only one. It runs after a merge, on schedule, or with the `tests:run-cloud` label.
- CI: the single-node integration job has 4 undici entries (Node 22/24/26 with ClickHouse `latest`, and Node 24 with `head`). One of them uploads coverage with the new `node-integration-undici` Codecov flag (`after_n_builds` is now 6).
- Tests of `node:http`-only features (`eagerly_destroy_stale_sockets`, the idle socket TTL suggestion) are skipped with the undici transport.
- The `ECONNRESET` socket test depends on the `sleep(0)` timing of the `node:http` transport. It now also checks `code === "ECONNRESET"` for both transports, and keeps its message check for `node:http`.
- `node_undici_transport.test.ts`: unit tests with a local HTTP server. They cover the option mapping, the error mapping, the native abort cases, the `destroy()` workaround, compression, auth, the summary, the Bun guard and the connection guards.

## Known `node:http` bugs (not changed in this PR)

- A pre-aborted `abort_signal` is ignored: #1047.
- An abort while the response body streams is ignored, because the wrapper removes its listener when the headers arrive.
- `socket_pool.ts` adds its abort listener to the signal but removes it from the request, so the listener is never removed.
- `node_abort_request.test.ts` "cancels a select query while reading response" passes for the wrong reason: `chunk.json()` is called on an array of rows, so the test fails with a `TypeError` before it calls `abort()`.

## Other known differences

- `keep_alive.eagerly_destroy_stale_sockets` has no effect with undici.
- With undici, `X-ClickHouse-Progress` headers do not restart `request_timeout`: `headersTimeout` is the total time until all the response headers arrive. A long-running query that returns its first rows late needs a longer `request_timeout` (documented).
- An application with another undici major version can install the client, but can use only the default transport.
- For a pre-aborted signal, undici opens a TCP connection but does not send the request.

## Status (draft)

- [x] CI passes (54/54), `codecov/patch` 92.93%
- [x] Unit tests pass with both transports (also on Bun, where the undici tests are skipped)
- [x] The undici entry point works in native ESM (`@clickhouse/client/undici/index.js`)
- [x] The cloud tests (`tests-cloud.yml`) pass with one Node.js 24 job with the undici transport too (HTTPS with a public certificate, a real load balancer, JWT auth): 324 passed, 49 skipped; the `http` job: 328 passed, 45 skipped. The 4 extra skips are the two `node:http`-only test files. Last run: 91bc151 (with the review fixes), the same counts
- [ ] A load test of the #294 stale-socket scenario with undici
- [ ] Streamed inserts are about 3.7× slower with undici, because the encoder sends one chunk per row and undici makes one socket write per chunk. The fix is in the encoder for both transports: #1133
- [ ] Removing `socket_pool.ts` later depends on the official Bun support decision

## Checklist

- [x] A human-readable description of the changes was provided to include in CHANGELOG
