title: v2: transport-independent error types for both clients
body:
## Summary

For v2, define error types that do not depend on the HTTP transport, and use the same error types in `@clickhouse/client` (Node.js) and `@clickhouse/client-web`.

## Problem

Today, the error contract of the Node.js client is the behavior of the `node:http` module: its messages and its Node.js error codes. Examples:

| Failure | Error today |
|---|---|
| The user aborts the request | `Error: The user aborted a request.`, or `AbortError` before the request is sent |
| `request_timeout` | `Error: Timeout error.` |
| The server closes the connection before the response headers | `Error: socket hang up`, `code: "ECONNRESET"` |
| The server closes the connection while the body streams | `Error: aborted`, `code: "ECONNRESET"` |
| The response headers are too large | `code: "HPE_HEADER_OVERFLOW"` |

User code checks these values, for example `err.code === "ECONNRESET"` in retry logic, and our docs name them (`docs/socket_hang_up_econnreset.md`, `max_response_headers_size`).

Each new transport must copy this behavior:
- The optional undici transport (#1128) maps each undici error to the `node:http` error, with the undici error in `cause`. undici 8 does not set the `HPE_*` code of parser errors, so that code is missing with undici.
- A transport for Bun (#1128 discussion) or the Web client (`fetch()`) gives other errors again.
- The Web client already has its own errors, for example its own abort message (#1118).

## Proposal (breaking, for v2)

1. **Abort:** an error with `name: "AbortError"` (the web-platform name), with the signal `reason` in `cause`.
2. **Timeout:** an error with `name: "TimeoutError"`.
3. **Connection errors:** one client error type with a small, documented set of `code` values, for example "connection closed", "connection refused" and "response headers too large". The transport error is in `cause`.
4. The same error types in the Node.js client and the Web client.
5. Each transport maps its errors to these types. Tests check the mapping for each transport.

`fetch()` (Web, Bun) and undici already use `AbortError` and `TimeoutError`, so items 1 and 2 are close to the platform behavior.

## Migration

- Users who check `err.code === "ECONNRESET"` or the messages above must change their code. The migration notes must list the old and the new values.
- Until v2, the current errors stay the contract for every transport (see #1128).

## Related

- #511: replace the `http`/`https` modules
- #1128: optional undici transport, with the error mapping to the current contract
- #1118: abort handling in the Web client

title: RowBinary: a bare Enum(...) type string is always folded to an 8-bit reader, so large ordinals desync the stream
fix(rowbinary): size a bare Enum(...) from its ordinals
body:
## Summary

Fixes #1130.

`astToReader` only looked at the type name to decide the enum width, so a bare `Enum(...)` always got read as 8-bit. But the server sizes a bare `Enum` based on its values. So for `Enum('a' = 1000)` the server sends 2 bytes, we read 1, get `"-24"`, and everything after it is off by a byte.

The fix: for a bare `Enum`, use `Enum16` if any value is outside `-128..127`, otherwise `Enum8`, which matches what the server does. Explicit `Enum8`/`Enum16` work the same as before.

## Testing

Added tests to `tests/compile.test.ts` based on the repro in the issue (values 1000, 128 and -129, a small-value case, and the two-column case). They fail without the fix, the same way the issue describes, and pass with it. I ran them against an embedded ClickHouse (26.9), not a full server, so CI is the real check there. Type-check and prettier pass.

## Checklist

- [x] Tests added
- [x] Changelog entry added in `skills/clickhouse-js-node-rowbinary/CHANGELOG.md` (I guessed 0.2.1, feel free to move it)

I used Claude Code to help with this. I reviewed it and ran the checks myself.

title: fix(parser): reject malformed DateTime64 precision and timezone
body:
## Summary

`parseColumnType` / `parseDateTime64Type` in `packages/client-common/src/parse/column_types.ts` (the shared parser bundled into both clients) accepted malformed `DateTime64` type strings and returned valid-looking parsed values:

- `DateTime64(10)` parsed as `{ precision: 1, timezone: "" }` instead of throwing.
- `DateTime64(12, 'UTC')` parsed as `{ precision: 1, timezone: "'UTC" }` (leading apostrophe kept, precision truncated).

Because `parseColumnType` is public API (exported from `@clickhouse/client` and `@clickhouse/client-web` since #316) and downstream code may feed it arbitrary strings, returning a silently different, valid-looking type is worse than throwing.

This PR parses the parameter list between the outer parens instead of fixed offsets: the precision token must be exactly one digit in `0..9`, and the timezone argument (when present) must be a single-quoted string. Anything else now throws a `ColumnTypeParseError`.

Fixes #1127

## Checklist

- [x] Unit and integration tests covering the common scenarios were added
- [x] A human-readable changelog entry was added to every affected package's `CHANGELOG.md` (client-node and client-web)
- [ ] For significant changes, documentation in https://github.com/ClickHouse/clickhouse-docs was updated with further explanations or tutorials (not needed: bug fix, no behavior change for well-formed input)

## Validation

- `npx vitest run parse_column_types_datetime` (client-node): 8 passed
- `npx vitest run column_types` (client-node): 40 passed
- `npx tsc --noEmit` (client-common): clean
- `npx eslint --max-warnings=0 src/parse/column_types.ts`: clean
- `npx prettier --check` on the changed files: clean

Note: the two changed files were reformatted with prettier; the toolchain used Node 24.22.1 against the repository's workspace (Windows, `core.symlinks=true` re-created for `packages/*/src/common`, which is required for the workspace to resolve `./common/index`).

## Compatibility

- No changes for well-formed input: `DateTime64(0..9)`, with or without a quoted timezone, parses exactly as before (all pre-existing parser tests pass unchanged).
- Malformed input now throws instead of returning a silently wrong value: `DateTime64(10)`, `DateTime64(12, 'UTC')`, unquoted/empty/garbage timezone arguments, and unterminated parameter lists throw a `ColumnTypeParseError`. This is a deliberate tightening of the parser contract for garbage input.
- The deprecated `parseColumnType`/`parseDateTime64Type` surface is unchanged in shape; no exports added or removed.

title: perf(node): streamed inserts send one chunk per row; write the encoded rows in frames
body:
## Summary

A streamed insert in the Node.js client sends **one chunk per row** to the HTTP transport. Best practice (the official ClickHouse Rust client, the Elasticsearch JS client, the Node.js stream docs) is to write the encoded rows into a buffer, and to send **frames of about 128–256 KiB**. With frames, a streamed insert uses **10 to 40 times less CPU** with both transports. The wall time is about **2× better** with `node:http`, and about **3.5× better** with the undici transport (#1128).

Suggested order:
1. Fix it for the default `node:http` transport. Users get the gain now.
2. Then use the same encoder in the undici transport (#1128), which needs it most.

The Web client is not affected (see "Scope").

## Problem

`NodeValuesEncoder.encodeValues()` maps each row of an object-mode stream to its own chunk (`mapStream()` in `packages/client-node/src/utils/stream.ts`). A row such as `{"n":1}` is about 12 bytes, so a 1M-row insert gives 1M chunks of about 12 bytes.

What the transports do with these chunks:

- **`node:http`** merges the chunks that are written while the socket is corked. This was fixed in Node.js core: nodejs/performance#57, fixed by nodejs/node#50167. So the cost is hidden, but each row still goes through the stream machinery one by one.
- **undici** (the optional transport in #1128) does `cork()`, writes the chunk header and the chunk, then `uncork()` at once, for each chunk (`AsyncWriter.write()` in `lib/dispatcher/client-h1.js`). nodejs/undici#1982 added the cork so that the headers and one chunk share a packet. undici does not merge several chunks. So each row is **one socket write**.

Measured with 100k rows into a ClickHouse `Null` table (Node.js 22.23, undici 8.12.3, ClickHouse 26.9, loopback):

| | Wall time | CPU (of it, system) | Socket writes | Bytes per write |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `node:http` | 90 ms | 108 ms (14 ms) | 53 | ~31,900 |
| undici | 263 ms | 305 ms (179 ms) | 100,001 | 17 |

With 1M rows: about 0.66 s with `node:http` and about 2.5 s with undici (3 of 3 runs). An insert of the same rows as **one array** is equally fast with both transports, because the encoder sends one string body.

## What frames give (plain transports, 100k rows, encoding included, 3 runs)

| Chunks | `node:http` (wall / CPU) | undici (wall / CPU) |
|---|---|---|
| one per row (today) | 122–145 ms / 71–119 ms | 214–302 ms / 212–278 ms |
| 64 KiB frames | 66–74 ms / 4–9 ms | 59–74 ms / 4–6 ms |
| 256 KiB frames | 73–76 ms / 8–10 ms | 59–74 ms / 5–9 ms |

With frames, both transports have about the same time, and the server is the limit.

## Best practice in other clients

| Client | What it does |
|---|---|
| ClickHouse **Rust** client (official, streams the insert over HTTP like this client) | Writes the serialized rows into a buffer, and sends a frame when the buffer reaches about 254 KiB (`BUFFER_SIZE = 256 * 1024`, `MIN_CHUNK_SIZE = BUFFER_SIZE - 2048`), and the rest at `end()`. There is no time-based flush. The maintainer chose the size by benchmark: "128KiB is the most appropriate buffer", because smaller chunks mean "more syscalls (more `write()`) and allocations" (ClickHouse/clickhouse-rs#17) |
| **Elasticsearch** JS client (built on undici) | The bulk helper batches by size (`flushBytes`, default 5 MB) **and** by time (`flushInterval`, default 30 s), whichever comes first |
| ClickHouse **Go** client | Collects rows in a batch and sends it with `Send()`, with an optional `Flush()` |
| **Node.js stream docs** | `cork()` is for "several small chunks … written in rapid succession", and the docs say to defer `uncork()` with `process.nextTick()`, so that all writes of one event-loop phase are batched. The code that writes is responsible for the batching, not the destination |

## Proposal

Change the Node.js value encoder so that it writes the encoded rows into a buffer and emits **frames** instead of one chunk per row:

- Emit a frame when the buffer reaches the frame size (128 KiB or 256 KiB; both were about equally fast).
- Emit the rest when the source ends.
- At most one frame per insert is buffered, so memory stays bounded. Backpressure from the transport stops reading from the source, as today.
- An error in the source or in the encoding still fails the insert.

The batching is in the encoder, so it does not depend on the transport: `node:http`, undici, and a later transport (for example for Bun) all get the same large chunks. The transports need no custom batching code.

### A slow source: two options

A source can produce rows slowly, for example a stream that gets an event every few seconds. A frame must not hold rows back forever.

| | Option A: flush by time | Option B: flush a partly filled frame when the source has no row ready |
|---|---|---|
| Rule | Emit the frame when it is full, **or** after a fixed time (for example 100 ms) since the first row in the frame | Emit the frame when it is full, **or** when the source has no more rows ready at the moment (it would wait for new data) |
| Example | Elasticsearch `flushInterval` | Close to the Node.js docs advice: batch what arrives in one event-loop phase |
| Extra delay for a slow source | up to the interval for each row | none: a row goes out as soon as the source pauses |
| Frames with a fast source | full | full (the source always has rows ready) |
| Frames with a source that produces rows one at a time, without a pause | full | can be small (one row per event-loop turn), so there is less gain |
| Extra code | a timer for each insert (clear it at the end, and on errors and aborts; `unref()` it) | no timer, but the encoder must know when the source is waiting (for example a `read()` that returns `null`, or a pause in the `for await` loop) |
| New option for users? | probably (the interval) | no |

### Open points

- **Raw streams** (not object mode, for example CSV or TSV): the encoder passes them unchanged today, so the chunk size is the user's choice. A stream with one line per chunk has the same problem: 100k TSV lines take 120–128 ms with `node:http` and 210–305 ms with undici. Should the encoder also put these into frames, or should the docs only recommend larger chunks?
- `exec()` with `values` also sends the user's stream unchanged.
- The frame size: 128 KiB or 256 KiB.

## Scope

- **Node.js client:** yes. Object-mode streams with JSON formats for sure; raw streams are an open point (see above).
- **Web client:** not affected. It does not support streamed inserts (`"Streaming is not supported for inserts in the web version of the client"`), so it always sends one string body. If the Web client adds streamed inserts later, it should use the same frames.
- **Array inserts:** not affected (one string body).

## Tests to add

- The number of chunks (or socket writes) for a 100k-row stream: a few frames, not one per row.
- A slow source: each row reaches the server within the agreed delay (option A: the interval; option B: at once when the source pauses).
- Memory: a large stream does not buffer more than one frame.
- Errors: an error in the source, and an encoding error (for example a circular object), fail the insert, also in the middle of a frame.
- Abort: an abort in the middle of a frame stops the insert, and does not leave a timer (option A).
- The same results with both transports (`CLICKHOUSE_TEST_TRANSPORT=undici`).

## Related

- #1128: optional undici transport. There, this is a 3.7× slowdown for streamed inserts.
- #511: replace the `http` / `https` modules.

## Sources

- nodejs/undici#1982: perf: cork socket before writing
- nodejs/performance#57: Merge HTTP chunks during chunked encoding (fixed by nodejs/node#50167)
- Node.js stream docs: `writable.cork()`, `writable.uncork()`: https://nodejs.org/api/stream.html
- Elasticsearch JS client helpers (`flushBytes`, `flushInterval`): https://www.elastic.co/docs/reference/elasticsearch/clients/javascript/client-helpers
- ClickHouse Rust client, `insert.rs`: https://docs.rs/clickhouse/latest/src/clickhouse/insert.rs.html
- ClickHouse/clickhouse-rs#17: insert chunk size
- ClickHouse Go client: https://clickhouse.com/docs/integrations/language-clients/go/clickhouse-api

## Summary

Adds `.claude/skills/issue-priority/SKILL.md`: the rules for the org issue field **Priority** (`Urgent`, `High`, `Medium`, `Low`) on clickhouse-js issues. A maintainer asked for the rules to live in this repo, so that people and automated triage use the same source. The root `AGENTS.md` points to it, like `RELEASING.md` points to the `release` skill.

The rules:

- **Base level** = reach tier × severity. The reach tier (Core, Common, Narrow, Satellite) comes from the most-used public path that reaches the defect, not from the file that contains it. This is because `packages/client-common/src` is linked into both clients.
- **Modifiers**, in this order:
  - security with a shown path from untrusted input: `Urgent` at any reach;
  - a regression in the latest release of the package: up one level;
  - a customer request linked from Linear: up one level, never to `Urgent`.
- **Confidence**: a missing reproduction lowers the confidence, not the level.
- **No priority** for issues that can be closed with no further action, for defects that only a deprecated API reaches, and for questions, CI, or release-process issues.
- **`@clickhouse/rowbinary` fixes** need a changelog line that tells users to regenerate their generated codecs. The skill copies reader and writer code into user projects, so a new release does not fix code that users already generated.

title: fix(client-web): cancel every request that shares an abort signal
body:
Fixes #1135

## Summary

`WebConnection.request` assigned the caller's `abort_signal.onabort` for every request. That property holds one handler. A signal shared by concurrent `query`, `command`, `exec`, or `insert` calls therefore cancelled only the request that started last, and a handler the caller had set on `signal.onabort` did not run.

The web client now subscribes with `addEventListener("abort", ...)` and removes that listener when the request is finished. For a response whose body is returned to the caller, the listener stays until that body ends, fails, or is cancelled, so an abort while the body is being read still cancels the read. This matches `@clickhouse/client`. A user abort still rejects with `The user aborted a request.`, and `request_timeout` still rejects with `Timeout error.`.

## Test plan

`packages/client-web/__tests__/unit/web_shared_abort_signal.test.ts` runs in Vitest (Chromium) with a stub `fetch` and no ClickHouse server. On main, 3 tests fail and 2 pass. With this change, 5 pass. The client-web unit suite (281 tests) also passes.

The failing case on main is two in-flight `command` calls that share one `AbortController`. Aborting that controller must reject both with `The user aborted a request.`, and a function assigned to `signal.onabort` before the calls must still run. On main the earlier call is not cancelled.

## Checklist

- [x] Unit tests covering a shared signal, a caller `onabort` handler, abort during a body read, and listener removal were added
- [x] A changelog entry was added to `packages/client-web/CHANGELOG.md`

This change was prepared with the assistance of an AI coding tool.

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **Low Risk**
> Localized web connection abort handling with targeted unit tests; no auth or data-path logic changes beyond correct cancellation semantics.
> 
> **Overview**
> Fixes **#1135** by changing how `@clickhouse/client-web` wires caller `abort_signal` into `WebConnection.request`. The client no longer assigns **`signal.onabort`** (which only holds one handler and was overwritten by each concurrent `query`/`command`/`exec`/`insert`). It now **`addEventListener("abort", …)`** per request, removes the listener when the request settles, and still rejects user aborts with **`The user aborted a request.`**.
> 
> For successful responses whose body is returned to the caller, the abort listener stays attached until the stream **ends, errors, or is cancelled** via new helpers **`bodyThatReleasesOnSettle`** / **`responseWithBodyThatReleases`**, so aborting while consuming a query stream still cancels the read. **Unit tests** in `web_shared_abort_signal.test.ts` cover shared signals, caller `onabort`, mid-stream abort, and listener cleanup; **CHANGELOG** documents the web-only behavior change.
>

fix(client-node): coalesce object-mode insert rows into larger HTTP chunks
body:
## summary

closes #988

an insert from an object-mode stream sends each row as a separate HTTP chunk. each chunk adds about 5 bytes of framing, and the stream code and the HTTP code handle the rows one at a time. for small rows, the request body is about 50% larger. with request compression, each row is a separate write into the zlib stream

`mapStream` now collects the encoded rows in a batch. it sends the batch when the batch reaches about 64 Ki characters (UTF-16, checked after the row is added), at the end of the current turn of the event loop, or when the stream ends. the rows that arrive in the same turn of the event loop make one batch. this is the plan jkugsiya posted on #988, and recommendations 1 to 4 of ccoltx's comment there. the end-of-turn send keeps a slow source from holding its rows while the server waits for the request body. when the output buffer is full, the stream sends the batch from the transform callback, so a slow consumer still stops the source

measured with a raw TCP sink: 1000 rows of `{ x: i }` in `JSONEachRow` (payload 9,890 bytes)

| input | chunks before | wire bytes before | chunks after | wire bytes after |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| array of 1000 objects | 1 | 9,903 | 1 | 9,903 |
| object-mode stream, no compression | 1000 | 14,895 (+50.6%) | 1 | 9,903 (+0.1%) |
| object-mode stream, gzip | 2 | 2,000 | 2 | 2,000 |

the gzip row has the same bytes on the wire, but not the same CPU time. ccoltx's measurements on this PR with 1M small rows on Node.js 22: 7,232 chunks instead of 1,000,000, client CPU 0.29 s instead of 0.94 s, and a gzip insert into a `Null` table in 0.46 s instead of 6.9 s. their measurements on #988 show the same for the undici transport in #1128

## scope

- object-mode streams only (`JSONEachRow` and the other JSON formats). raw-format streams (CSV, TSV, RowBinary) that push small pieces are not changed (point 6 on #988 is still open). a change in `mapStream` works with both transports, so `socket_pool.ts`, which #1128 changes, is not touched
- a row the serializer cannot encode (eg a `BigInt` value or an object with a circular reference) now fails the stream through the transform callback, and the rows in the batch are dropped (point 5 on #988). on `main` with Node.js 22 the throw is an uncaught exception and the process exits with code 1. Node.js 24 and 26 already pass the error to the pipeline. a value thrown by a custom `json.stringify` that is not an `Error` (eg `undefined` or `null`) is wrapped into an `Error`, so it cannot read as success
- the readable side keeps at most one batch (`readableHighWaterMark: 1`), so an insert that waits for a socket does not hold 16 batches

## testing

- new unit tests in `node_mapStream.test.ts` and `node_insert_stream_chunks.test.ts`, no ClickHouse server needed. they cover the batch size, a slow source, a slow consumer, gzip, a source error, a row that cannot be encoded, a mapper that throws a value that is not an `Error`, and a destroyed stream with rows in the batch
- one new integration test in `node_stream_json_insert.test.ts`: a `BigInt` row in the middle of a stream makes the insert reject with the `TypeError`, the table has no rows, and the next query on the same client works
- checked before the merge of `main`: build, typecheck, lint with `--max-warnings=0`, prettier, and `npm run test:node:unit` (445 passed, 4 skipped)
- the review fixes: prettier, and the changed `mapStream` run on its own with Node.js 26. before the fix, a mapper that throws `undefined`, `null`, `0` or `false` lets the pipeline resolve, and one that throws a string rejects with the string. after the fix, all five reject with an `Error`
- integration tests not run locally (no docker). ccoltx ran them on Node.js 22 after the merge of `main`

AI tools assisted with this change

## Checklist

- [x] Unit tests covering the common scenarios were added, plus one integration test for a row that cannot be encoded
- [x] A human-readable changelog entry was added to every affected package's `CHANGELOG.md` (`packages/client-node/CHANGELOG.md`; the change affects only the Node.js client)

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **Medium Risk**
> Touches the hot path for JSON stream inserts via `mapStream` in the encoder, but behavior is constrained to object-mode streams and is covered by new unit and integration tests.
> 
> **Overview**
> **Object-mode inserts** (e.g. `JSONEachRow` via a `Readable` stream) no longer emit one HTTP chunk per row. `mapStream` now **accumulates encoded rows** and flushes when the batch hits ~64 Ki UTF-16 characters, at the end of the current event-loop turn (so slow producers still ship data), or on stream end—cutting framing overhead and greatly speeding gzip stream inserts.
> 
> Encoding failures (**`BigInt`**, circular references, or a mapper throwing non-`Error` values) now **reject the insert** through the transform callback instead of risking an uncaught exception on Node.js 22; partial batches after an error are dropped. Output still uses **`Buffer`** batches (unchanged workaround for Node 24/26 non-ASCII `ClientRequest` issues).
> 
> Changelog entries and new unit/integration tests cover chunk coalescing, slow sources/consumers, compression, and mid-stream encode failures.

title: Security: quote table and column identifiers in insert() SQL generation
body:
## 背景

`insert()` 方法在生成 `INSERT INTO ... FORMAT ...` SQL 时，直接将 `params.table` 和 `params.columns` / `params.columns.except` 数组中的每个字段用字符串拼接方式插入 SQL，没有做任何标识符 quoting 或转义。

攻击者（或调用方）可以通过构造恶意的 table / columns 参数实现 SQL 注入，例如：

`js
await client.insert({
  table: 't FORMAT JSONEachRow; DROP TABLE users --',
  values: [],
});
// 生成: INSERT INTO t FORMAT JSONEachRow; DROP TABLE users -- FORMAT JSONEachRow
// 分号前的部分就是一个合法的 INSERT，ClickHouse 会把它当作第一条语句执行
`

## 修复

在 `packages/client-common/src/client.ts` 中新增 `quoteIdentifier` 辅助函数：

- 使用反引号 `  ` 包裹每个标识符（ClickHouse 标准 quoting 方式）；
- 对标识符内部的反引号做转义（ClickHouse 的转义规则是重复反引号：`  ` → ` ` `）；
- 对带点号的限定名 `db.table` 按 `.` 分割，每部分分别 quoting，生成 `\db\.\	able\`，保持跨库引用语义不变。

然后将它应用到 `getInsertQuery` 函数里的三处拼接：table、columns 数组、EXCEPT 数组。

## 变更影响

- 正常标识符（不含特殊字符）加上反引号后 ClickHouse 行为完全相同，向后兼容；
- `db.table` 形式会变成 `\db\.\	able\`，同样正确；
- 含反引号的标识符会被正确转义；
- 恶意注入代码会被当作反引号包裹的标识符名，不会被当作 SQL 执行。

## 测试

在本地 Node.js 环境下用脚本覆盖了 11 个场景（简单表名、db.table、三部分限定名、反引号转义、含空格、列数组、EXCEPT、SQL 注入尝试等），全部通过。

## 涉及文件

- `packages/client-common/src/client.ts` — 新增 `quoteIdentifier` 并应用于 `getInsertQuery`
- `packages/client-node/CHANGELOG.md` — 变更记录
- `packages/client-web/CHANGELOG.md` — 变更记录（client-common 的代码被打包进两个客户端）

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **High Risk**
> Security fix for SQL injection via `insert()` parameters when table/column names are attacker-controlled or untrusted; low runtime risk for typical static identifiers but high importance for deployment.
> 
> **Overview**
> **Fixes SQL injection in `insert()`** by adding a `quoteIdentifier` helper in shared client code and using it when building `INSERT INTO ... FORMAT ...` statements.
> 
> Table names (`InsertParams.table`), explicit column lists, and `columns.except` entries are now wrapped in ClickHouse backticks, with embedded backticks doubled. Qualified names like `db.table` are quoted as `` `db`.`table` `` instead of being pasted verbatim.
> 
> The **Node and Web client changelogs** document this as a security bug fix: malicious `table`/`columns` values could previously append extra SQL (e.g. semicolon-separated statements). Normal identifier usage should behave the same once quoted.
> 
> <sup>Reviewed by [Cursor Bugbot](https://cursor.com/bugbot) for commit 4e1ef8beeaa1519fc0b0472ee48eac12eef68bff. Bugbot is set up for automated code reviews on this repo. Configure [here](https://www.cursor.com/dashboard/bugbot).</sup>

title: test(client-node): add integration tests for large object-mode stream inserts
body:
## Summary

The integration tests for object-mode stream inserts send at most 5 rows. With such small data, the tests do not use the code that sends a large stream, and they cannot find data loss in it. #1141 (for #988) changes this code: it collects the rows in batches before the HTTP request. This PR adds integration tests that check the data that the server gets from large object-mode streams. They pass on `main`, and they must also pass after #1141. #1141 can merge `main` after this PR to get them.

The tests check the rows in the table, not the HTTP chunks, because the server does not show the chunk boundaries. #1141 has unit tests with a raw TCP sink for the chunks.

New tests in `node_stream_json_insert.test.ts` (no new test file, so no new database on cloud):

- 50,000 rows, without and with request compression
- 50,000 rows with multi-byte characters
- rows larger than 64 KiB between small rows
- a source that pauses between the rows
- three streams that wait for one connection (`max_open_connections: 1`)
- a source error, and an abort, in the middle of a stream: the insert rejects, and the table has no rows

Each insert has fewer rows than one server insert block (`max_insert_block_size`). For this reason, a failed insert must leave no rows.

No changelog entry: this PR changes only tests.

## Testing

- Local ClickHouse 26.11, Node.js 22.23: the spec passes on `main` (12 of 12). With the changes of #1141 applied, the spec passes, and the full Node.js integration suite passes (363 passed, 18 skipped).
- With #1141, the new tests reach all the send paths of the batching code: a full batch, a full output buffer, the end of an event-loop turn, and the end of the stream. The existing tests reached only the last two, with at most 189 characters.
- Mutation check on #1141: when the code loses the last batch, loses full batches, loses the batches of a full output buffer, or sends a batch twice, some of the new tests fail. A change that only holds the rows until the end of the stream does not make them fail, as expected. Only a wire-level test can see that.
- The test log shows `Error: The source failed` and some other errors. The existing `console.error` in `NodeValuesEncoder` (`pipelineCb`, marked FIXME) prints them. They are not failures.
- Cloud: the `tests:run-cloud` label is added to run the tests on cloud.

## Checklist

- [x] Unit and integration tests covering the common scenarios were added (integration tests only; this PR changes no source code)

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

---

> **Low Risk**
> Test-only changes with no production code; risk is limited to longer or heavier integration runs in CI.
> 
> **Overview**
> Adds a **`large object-mode streams`** `describe` block to `node_stream_json_insert.test.ts` so JSONEachRow inserts are exercised at scales the previous cases (≤5 rows) never hit—intended as a gate for batching/send-path changes such as #1141.
> 
> New cases cover **50,000-row** happy paths (plain and request-compressed), Unicode payloads, **>64 KiB** rows mixed with small ones, slow/async sources, and three concurrent inserts on **`max_open_connections: 1`**. Failure behavior asserts **all-or-nothing**: mid-stream **source errors** and **`abort_signal`** aborts must reject the insert and leave **zero rows** when row count stays below one server insert block. Helpers (`makeRows`, `selectAll`, `countRows`) plus `sleep`/`describe` imports support timing-sensitive scenarios.

title: ci: run the Prettier check for every PR
body:
## Summary

The `code-quality` job in `tests-node.yml` ran the Prettier check. That workflow runs only when the packages, the tests, or the build config change. A PR that changed only other files (agent skills, docs, examples, workflows) was not checked. Because `npm run prettier:check` covers the whole repository, the next PR that changed a package then failed for a file that it did not change.

This occurred after #1136: the table in `.claude/skills/issue-priority/SKILL.md` is not formatted, and `code-quality` now fails for every package PR (for example #1143). The pre-commit hook formats `*.md`, but the commit of #1136 came from a bot that did not run the hook.

This PR:

- formats `.claude/skills/issue-priority/SKILL.md` (4 lines in one table)
- adds `.github/workflows/format.yml`: the same Prettier step, without a `paths` filter. It runs for every PR and for every push to `main` and `release`. It needs only `npm ci --ignore-scripts`, not a build.
- removes the Prettier step from `tests-node.yml`, so the check runs once
- adds one sentence about the new workflow to `CONTRIBUTING.md`

Other options that we did not use:

- add the other paths to `tests-node.yml`: a docs-only PR would then run the full Node.js test matrix
- exclude the skills from Prettier: this fixes only one of the paths that were not checked, and the pre-commit hook formats them anyway

No ruleset requires the `code-quality` check by name (the only required workflow is `ai-gate-required.yml`), so no ruleset change is necessary.

No changelog entry: this PR changes no package.

## Testing

- `npm ci --ignore-scripts` and `npm run prettier:check`: all files pass after the fix. Before the fix, only `.claude/skills/issue-priority/SKILL.md` failed.
- The new `format` workflow ran on this PR and passed. The `node` workflow also runs on this PR, because the PR changes `tests-node.yml` (that file is in its `paths` filter). On a later PR that changes only docs, skills, or other workflows, only `format` runs.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> **Low Risk**
> CI and documentation-only changes; no runtime or application code affected.
> 
> **Overview**
> **Prettier now runs in a standalone `format` workflow on every PR and push to `main`/`release`**, so docs-, skills-, and workflow-only changes get checked instead of slipping through until a package PR fails on unrelated files.
> 
> The check is **removed from `tests-node.yml`**’s `code-quality` job (no duplicate runs). The new workflow uses `npm ci --ignore-scripts` only—no build—and reuses the same `prettier:check` error reporting as before.

title: fix(rowbinary): resolve names of Enum elements without numbers
body:
## Summary

Fixes #1138 (the `@clickhouse/rowbinary` part, as the triage comment recommends).

A hand-written type string such as `Enum8('a', 'b')` has no numbers. The parser gives a generic `DataType` node for it, the same as the server AST. The fold in `compile.ts` then used `readEnum8(new Map())`, so the reader returned the stringified number (`"2"` for `'b'`) with no error. `Enum('a', 'b')` had no case in the fold and failed with `unsupported RowBinary type: Enum`.

What changes:

- The `Enum8` and `Enum16` cases build the name map from the arguments of the node. The numbers follow the server (`autoAssignNumberForEnum`): the element at position `i` gets `base + i`, where `base` is the number of the first element, or 1 when the first element has none.
- A new `Enum` case does the same and reads the value as `Enum16` when a number does not fit in `Int8`. That is how the server stores `Enum(...)`.

What stays the same:

- `@clickhouse/datatype-parser` and its AST are not changed.
- `Enum8` and `Enum16` with no arguments still return the stringified number, and `Enum` with no arguments still throws `RowBinaryTypeError`.
- The `EnumDataType` case (all numbers explicit) is not touched, so this does not overlap with #1131.
- `parseColumnType` is deprecated, so I did not change it.

The server accepts only two forms without full numbers: no element has a number, or only the first element has one. I checked the rule against 26.9 with `toTypeName(defaultValueOfTypeName(...))` for each form in the tests.

## Checklist

- [x] Unit and integration tests covering the common scenarios were added
- [x] A human-readable changelog entry was added to every affected package's `CHANGELOG.md` (e.g. `packages/client-node/CHANGELOG.md`; a shared/common change updates both client packages — `client-node` and `client-web`; the root `CHANGELOG.md` is frozen)

`tests/compile.test.ts` has 10 new cases. Each one decodes `FORMAT RowBinary` bytes from the live server. 8 of them fail on `main`. The other 2 pin the behavior that does not change (`Enum8` and `Enum` with no arguments). The full rowbinary suite passes against 26.9 (734 tests), and `tsc --noEmit` and `prettier --check` are clean.

I also ran the program from the triage comment against the built package:

| Type string | Server type | `main` | This PR |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Enum8('a', 'b')` | `Enum8('a' = 1, 'b' = 2)` | `"2"` | `"b"` |
| `Enum16('a', 'b')` | `Enum16('a' = 1, 'b' = 2)` | `"2"` | `"b"` |
| `Enum8('a' = 5, 'b')` | `Enum8('a' = 5, 'b' = 6)` | `"6"` | `"b"` |
| `Enum('a', 'b')` | `Enum8('a' = 1, 'b' = 2)` | `RowBinaryTypeError` | `"b"` |
| `Enum('a' = 127, 'b')` | `Enum16('a' = 127, 'b' = 128)` | `RowBinaryTypeError` | `"b"` |
| `Array(Enum8('a', 'b'))` | `Array(Enum8('a' = 1, 'b' = 2))` | `["2"]` | `["b"]` |

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **Low Risk**
> Targeted reader/compiler change for hand-written enum type strings, with broad integration tests; no parser or wire-format changes for normal server-provided types.
> 
> **Overview**
> Fixes RowBinary decoding when hand-written enum type strings omit numeric values. **`astToReader`** now builds name lookups with server-style auto-numbering (`base + i`, honoring an explicit first value) for `Enum8`, `Enum16`, and new **`Enum`** (choosing `Enum8` vs `Enum16` by range). Decoded values are element **names** instead of stringified ints; bare `Enum` no longer throws. Unchanged: empty `Enum8`/`Enum` argument lists and server types with explicit numbers.
> 
> Adds **`autoEnumNameMap`** in `compile.ts`, a **0.2.1** changelog note, and integration tests against live `FORMAT RowBinary` bytes (including arrays and edge cases like names containing `=`).
>

title: feat: add external_data (per-query temporary tables) support
body:
## Summary

Adds an `external_data` option to `query()`, `command()` and `exec()` in `@clickhouse/client` and `@clickhouse/client-web`. It attaches one or more temporary tables to a single request, with the ClickHouse HTTP feature [External data for query processing](https://clickhouse.com/docs/en/engines/table-engines/special/external-data).

Refs #356. That issue was closed as not planned, so I am glad to change the API or the scope if the maintainers prefer a different design.

## Design: based on the Python client

The design follows the Python client, [`clickhouse-connect`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/clickhouse-connect), which has this feature as the `external_data` argument ([`driver/external.py`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/clickhouse-connect/blob/main/clickhouse_connect/driver/external.py)). The aim is feature parity between the two clients.

| | `clickhouse-connect` | This PR |
|---|---|---|
| Option name | `external_data` | `external_data` |
| Table schema | `structure` or `types`, each a string or a list | the same |
| Format | `fmt`, optional, server default | `format`, optional, server default |
| Table data | one file part for each table, `application/octet-stream` | the same |
| Schema and format | `<name>_structure` / `<name>_types` / `<name>_format` in the URL | the same |
| Operations | query, command, raw query | `query()`, `command()`, `exec()` |

Differences from the Python client:

- The SQL goes in a `query` form field, not in the URL, to agree with `use_multipart_params` in this client.
- There is no `file_path` or `mime_type` option. In Node.js, `fs.createReadStream()` gives the same result as `file_path`.
- `data` also accepts a stream (Node.js only) and an array of rows for `JSON*` formats, to agree with `insert()`.

**Use case:** join a list of 100k+ ids in one stateless request. Today, the list must go in `query_params`, where `http_max_field_value_size` (128 KiB by default) limits each value, or in a temporary table, which needs a `session_id`.

```ts
const rs = await client.query({
  query: `
    SELECT e.id, e.value
    FROM events AS e
    INNER JOIN selected_ids AS s ON e.id = s.id
  `,
  format: "JSONEachRow",
  external_data: [
    {
      name: "selected_ids",
      structure: "id String",
      format: "TSV",
      data: ids.join("\n"),
    },
  ],
});
```

## API

Each entry has:

- `name`: the table name used in the SQL.
- `structure` (`'id String, n UInt32'` or `['id String', 'n UInt32']`) or `types` (`'String, UInt32'`, columns `_1`, `_2`, ...). Exactly one of the two.
- `format` (optional): the server default is `TabSeparated`.
- `data`: a `string`, a `Uint8Array` / `Buffer`, an array of rows for `JSON*` formats (encoded as in `insert()`), or (Node.js only) a `Stream.Readable`.

## Wire format

- Each table is a `multipart/form-data` file part named after the table.
- `<name>_structure` or `<name>_types`, and `<name>_format`, go in the URL.
- The SQL goes in a `query` form field, as it does for `use_multipart_params`. Bound `query_params` stay in the URL, or go in the form when `use_multipart_params` / `use_multipart_params_auto` selects that.
- Node.js streams the body when an entry is a stream. Other bodies are built in memory.

## Behavior to review

- **Request compression is off for these requests (Node.js).** The server does not decompress a `multipart/form-data` body: a gzip body gives `HTML Form Exception: No boundary line found`.
- **`exec()` rejects `values` together with `external_data`.** The two use the request body in different ways.
- **Web has no stream input**, the same as `insert()`. The types and a runtime check both reject a `ReadableStream`.
- **Web bug fix, not specific to this feature:** browsers reject a `fetch()` request that has `keepalive: true` and a body larger than 64 KiB (`TypeError: Failed to fetch`). The web client sets `keepalive` by default, so a large `query()` body failed before this PR too. The client now sends a request with a body larger than 64 KiB without the flag. I can move this fix to a separate PR.
- **Limit on the SQL text:** because the SQL is a form field, `http_max_field_value_size` limits its length for a request with `external_data`. The setting does not limit the tables. The docs state this.
- **Type exports:** `QueryParams`, `QueryParamsWithFormat`, `ExecParams` and `CommandParams` are now exported from each client package with the stream type of that platform, not re-exported from the common module.

## Tests

- Unit tests for validation, the multipart body, and the URL parameters (common, Node.js, Web).
- Integration tests, run on Node.js and in Chromium:
  - `structure` and `types`, each as a string and as an array
  - the default format, `TSV`, `CSV`, `JSONEachRow`, `JSONCompactEachRow`
  - several tables in one query, together with `query_params`
  - a 120,000-row table in one request with the default `http_max_field_value_size`
  - `command()`
- Node.js integration tests: `Buffer`, a byte stream, an object-mode JSON stream, a Parquet file stream, and a 105,000-row stream in `exec()` with request compression enabled in the client.

I ran the type check, lint, the unit tests of both packages, and the integration tests that this PR adds or changes, against ClickHouse 26.3.9.8. I did not run the full integration suites locally.

## Checklist

- [x] Unit and integration tests covering the common scenarios were added
- [x] A human-readable changelog entry was added to every affected package's `CHANGELOG.md` (`packages/client-node/CHANGELOG.md` and `packages/client-web/CHANGELOG.md`)
- [ ] For significant changes, documentation in https://github.com/ClickHouse/clickhouse-docs was updated with further explanations or tutorials. This PR updates `docs/clickhouse-docs/index.mdx`, the examples and the `clickhouse-js-node-coding` skill in this repository. I did not open a PR in `clickhouse-docs`.

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **Medium Risk**
> Changes the HTTP encoding path for core read/write operations (multipart bodies, compression, fetch keepalive), but scope is additive with substantial validation and test coverage rather than auth or payment logic.
> 
> **Overview**
> Adds **`external_data`** to `query()`, `command()`, and `exec()` on `@clickhouse/client` and `@clickhouse/client-web`, so callers can attach one or more **per-request temporary tables** over ClickHouse’s HTTP external-data flow (`multipart/form-data`), without `session_id` and without stuffing huge ID lists into `query_params` (bypassing the default 128 KiB `http_max_field_value_size` on param values).
> 
> Each **`ExternalDataEntry`** supplies `name`, `structure` or `types`, optional `format`, and `data` (string / `Uint8Array`, JSON row arrays, or on Node.js `Stream.Readable`). The shared layer validates names, encodes JSON rows, emits `<name>_structure|_types|_format` in the URL, and builds multipart bodies (including binary **`buildMultipartBytes`** and collision checks against settings). **Node** streams multipart when any table is a stream, turns off request compression for these requests, and wires stream lifecycle on abort/timeout/errors. **Web** uses in-memory multipart only (no `ReadableStream` for `external_data`, matching `insert()`), drops conflicting custom `content-type` on multipart requests, and disables **`keepalive`** when the body exceeds 64 KiB.
> 
> **`exec()`** cannot combine `values` and `external_data`. Public types for query/exec/command params are re-exported per package with platform stream types. Docs, examples, skills, integration/unit tests, and **1.26.0** changelog entries accompany the feature.
> 
> <sup>Reviewed by [Cursor Bugbot](https://cursor.com/bugbot) for commit 06ac211920117669bb816dc8c7f82f114225946d. Configure [here](https://www.cursor.com/dashboard/bugbot).</sup>
<!-- /CURSOR_SUMMARY -->

title: CHANGELOG.md: frozen-changelog banner links the @clickhouse/rowbinary changelog at a removed path (404)
body:
### Describe the bug

The banner at the top of the repository-wide `CHANGELOG.md` tells readers where new changelog entries now live. Its `@clickhouse/rowbinary` entry links to a path that does not exist on `main`, so the link returns 404 on GitHub:

https://github.com/ClickHouse/clickhouse-js/blob/7c2f320/CHANGELOG.md?plain=1#L9

title: fix(client-node): write Buffers to the request of an object-mode stream insert
body:
## Summary

Closes #1149

With Node.js 24 and 26, an insert from an object-mode stream (`JSONEachRow` and the other JSON formats) with non-ASCII text can stop after about 64 KiB of the request body. The insert then fails with a timeout. #1143 found this: its test "inserts rows with multi-byte characters" fails on ClickHouse Cloud with Node.js 24 and 26 ("Timeout exceeded while reading from socket ... 30000 ms"). It passes with Node.js 22.

### Cause

`mapStream` sends each encoded row as a string, and the request pipe writes the strings into `http.ClientRequest`. Since Node.js 24, `ClientRequest` collects the writes of one tick into one chunk (nodejs/node#64987):

- `write()` returns `false` when the collected data reaches 64 KiB. It counts the strings in **bytes** (`Buffer.byteLength`).
- The `'drain'` event comes when the socket emits `'drain'`. The socket counts strings in **characters**.

With non-ASCII text, a string has more bytes than characters. The request asks the writer to wait, but the socket is never full, so `'drain'` does not come and the pipe stops. At the stall, the request reports `writableNeedDrain: true` with `writableLength: 0`, and the socket is idle.

A script with only `node:http` and no client shows the same stall on Node.js 24.22 and 26.13: many small strings with `é` or CJK characters stall, and the same data as Buffers does not. Node.js 22 is not affected. Whether the stall occurs depends on the timing of the writes. It occurred every time in our local tests and on Cloud, but not with the local ClickHouse in CI.

### Fix

`mapStream` sends Buffers (`Buffer.from(mapper(chunk))`). The request and the socket then count the same bytes. Node.js converts a string to UTF-8 before it writes it to the socket anyway, so the extra cost is small.

Raw-format streams (CSV, TSV) usually send Buffers and are not changed. A raw stream that sends strings (for example, after `setEncoding()`) is not covered by this PR.

## Testing

- New unit test `node_insert_stream_non_ascii.test.ts`: it inserts 10,000 rows with two-byte characters, and with CJK characters and an emoji, into a raw TCP sink, and checks the complete body.
  - Without the fix: both cases fail on Node.js 24.22 and 26.13 (request timeout). They pass on Node.js 22.
  - With the fix: they pass on Node.js 22, 24 and 26.
- Full Node.js unit suite on Node.js 22: 434 passed, 7 skipped. Lint and typecheck pass.
- After this PR is merged, #1143 can merge `main` and run the Cloud tests again.

Related: #1141 rewrites `mapStream` (batching). It must keep sending Buffers. Batching alone does not prevent the stall.

## Checklist

- [x] Unit and integration tests covering the common scenarios were added (unit test; the integration test is in #1143)
- [x] A human-readable changelog entry was added to every affected package's `CHANGELOG.md` (`packages/client-node/CHANGELOG.md`; Node.js only)

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **Low Risk**
> Narrow fix to HTTP request encoding for object-mode JSON inserts; behavior is equivalent on Node 22 and aligns bytes on Node 24+ with minimal overhead.
> 
> **Overview**
> Fixes stream inserts (`JSONEachRow` and similar) that could **stall after ~64 KiB and time out** on **Node.js 24+** when rows contain non-ASCII text.
> 
> **`mapStream`** in `packages/client-node/src/utils/stream.ts` now pushes each serialized row as a **`Buffer`** instead of a string, so `http.ClientRequest` backpressure matches what the socket reports (Node 24+ counted string writes in bytes vs characters). Node.js 22 behavior is unchanged.
> 
> Adds unit coverage in `node_insert_stream_non_ascii.test.ts` (10k rows with multi-byte/CJK text via a raw TCP sink) and documents the fix in `CHANGELOG.md`.

body:
Bumps the dev-dependencies group with 2 updates: [playwright](https://github.com/microsoft/playwright) and [undici](https://github.com/nodejs/undici). Updates `playwright` from 1.64.1 to 1.65.0
Release notes

Sourced from playwright's releases.

v1.65.0

🥟 Run tests with Bun

The test runner now runs under Bun. Bun transpiles your TypeScript test files itself, so Playwright does not use Babel or its compilation cache. Pass the --bun flag, because without it bunx playwright test runs on Node.js:

bunx --bun playwright test

Our CI runs the test runner tests under Bun 1.4.3 on Linux. Some features work differently under Bun:

  • There is no watch mode. UI mode does not run tests again when files change, and --only-changed does not follow imports.
  • Bun loads modules itself, so --tsconfig and the JSX options in tsconfig.json have no effect, and custom ESM loaders are not supported.
  • Stack traces do not include async frames, and API names do not include the class name: click instead of locator.click. This changes some step locations, step titles and error messages.
  • Console output of a test does not get into the trace and UI mode.

🚨 Reports with only failures

New failures reporter prints failures and successful retries as they occur, followed by a summary, without progress output.

New onlyFailures option of the HTML, JSON and JUnit reporters keeps only tests with unexpected outcomes, flaky tests and interrupted tests:

// playwright.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
reporter: [
['failures'],
['html', { onlyFailures: true }],
],
});

🎯 Test runner

  • New built-in -exclusive- test lock runs a test only when no other tests are running. All other tests continue to run in parallel with each other:

    test('restart the server', { lock: '-exclusive-' }, async () => {
  // No other test runs while this one is running.
});

  • test.skip(), test.fixme(), test.fail() and test.slow() now accept only a description. It is recorded in the test annotation:

    test('upload a file', async ({ page }) => {
  test.skip('Not implemented yet');
});

Updates `undici` from 8.12.3 to 8.12.4
Release notes

Sourced from undici's releases.

v8.12.4

⚠️ Security Fixes

This release fixes six vulnerabilities.

CVE-2026-116592 / GHSA-mqg3-3v4r-cm32 (high)

Undici 8.12.2 and 8.12.3 could cache the final response from a redirect chain under the original request key without applying the origin, cache policy, freshness, or Vary requirements of every intermediate hop. This could poison a cache or expose one user's response to another user. The fix validates every redirect hop, combines their Vary fields, limits freshness and stale serving to the most restrictive hop, and invalidates persistent SQLite entries written by vulnerable releases.

CVE-2026-120474 / GHSA-7xg3-fphp-28hg (medium)

A shared cache used with compose(redirect(), cache()) could store a credential-dependent response from a same-origin redirect under the original URL. A later authenticated or unauthenticated request could then receive another user's response. Redirected requests carrying Authorization, Cookie, or Proxy-Authorization are no longer stored under the original alias key.

CVE-2026-116630 / GHSA-5rm8-gv32-r954 (medium)

A cross-origin redirect during cache revalidation could let a 304 Not Modified response from the redirect target validate a cached response from the original origin. Undici now checks that the revalidation target matches the cached URL and that any returned validator matches the stored representation before replaying the cached body.

CVE-2026-120415 / GHSA-9v6h-8rgp-m69f (medium)

The redirect interceptor did not strip credentials correctly when request headers were supplied as an array of [name, value] pairs. With a header-normalizing interceptor outside redirect(), credentials could be sent to a cross-origin redirect target. Undici now handles both tuple arrays and flat header arrays when removing sensitive headers.

CVE-2026-120222 / GHSA-3g9m-rv3r-w5w2 (medium)

A downstream handler exception during cache replay could escape as an uncaught exception or unhandled promise rejection and terminate the process. This included dump size-limit failures, excessive Content-Encoding values in decompress, asynchronous cache-store failures, and cached-body replay after a 304. These failures are now reported as request errors.

CVE-2026-120423 / GHSA-r4pc-4jcp-7pqc (medium)

fetch() could skip Subresource Integrity verification when valid integrity metadata was separated or surrounded by ASCII whitespace other than a space, including a horizontal tab. Integrity metadata is now split on all ASCII whitespace before SHA-256, SHA-384, or SHA-512 verification.

- it goes into a private GitHub vulnerability report for this repository (private vulnerability reporting is on), never into a public issue, comment, or pull request; the text of a public issue about it is copied into the report first;
- the public issue gets no Priority: it is closed with a comment that gives no details, and a repository administrator is asked to delete it, because closing does not hide its text;
- the rules of this skill still rate the vulnerability, and the level and its reason go into the private report as the proposed severity.

The impact Security now also names memory corruption, and says that a hang or a crash that only a hostile server or network causes is Stability. `AGENTS.md` gets one sentence after the issue-priority pointer: a vulnerability that is not public yet goes into a private security report, never into an issue or a pull request.

A vulnerability that is already public (a published CVE or GHSA, for example in a dependency) and an authentication method that does not work or is missing get a Priority as before. Modifier 1 now points to the new section in place of "a private channel".

No library code changes, so there is no changelog entry. `prettier --check` passes on the file.

## Summary

Follow-up to #1157 (merged). Cursor Bugbot found a new gap after each small fix, because some rules were in two to four places with different words. This PR states each rule in **one place**, and checks the result against a fixed case table.

- **Classification** (`.claude/skills/issue-classification/SKILL.md`): two new boundaries, **"Hostile server or network"** and **"Dependencies"**. The Security row and the list of "A vulnerability that is not public yet" point to them.
- **Priority** (`.claude/skills/issue-priority/SKILL.md`): the severity rows carry the rules. The first row covers a vulnerability in a dependency only when the client calls the vulnerable code. "Workaround exists" covers the impact Performance of a defect only. The last row names speed requests and dependency updates, also one for a dependency vulnerability in code that the client does not call. The section "Vulnerabilities that are not public yet" only points to the classification; the separate speed and dependency paragraphs are gone.

## Case table (expected outcome → the text gives it)

| Case | Classification | Public or private | Severity row |
|---|---|---|---|
| Request to make an operation faster | Performance | public | Cosmetic, docs, feature |
| Correct result, but too slow | Performance | public | Workaround exists |
| Missing authentication method | Security (authentication) | public | Cosmetic, docs, feature |
| Authentication method that does not work | Security (authentication) | public | by its failure |
| Secret that leaks (log, error, URL, other host) | Security (vulnerability) | private | Wrong data or security (proposed severity) |
| Hang, or crash with no memory corruption, only from a hostile server or network | Stability | public | by its failure |
| Memory corruption, also only from a hostile server or network | Security (vulnerability) | private | Wrong data or security (proposed severity) |
| Crash on server data, memory corruption not ruled out | not decided | private until decided | — |
| Published CVE or GHSA, client calls the code | Security (vulnerability) | public | Wrong data or security |
| Published CVE or GHSA, client does not call the code | none (dependency update) | public | Cosmetic, docs, feature |
| Unpublished dependency vulnerability, client calls the code | Security (vulnerability) | private | Wrong data or security (proposed severity) |
| Unpublished dependency vulnerability, client does not call the code | Security (vulnerability) | private | Cosmetic, docs, feature (proposed severity) |
| Vulnerability that only code inspection shows | as above | private | confidence `MEDIUM` |

title: fix(parseColumnType): decode NUL, backspace, form feed and control escapes in enum labels
body:
## Summary

`unescapeEnumName` in `packages/client-common/src/parse/column_types.ts` previously only decoded `\n`, `\t`, `\r`, `\\`, and `\'`, falling through to the `default` branch for all other escapes. When the ClickHouse server renders `Enum8`/`Enum16` type names via `writeAnyEscapedString`, it also emits `\0` (NUL), `\b` (backspace), `\f` (form feed), `\a` (bell), and `\v` (vertical tab). Those sequences were previously unescaped into literal characters (`0`, `b`, `f`, `a`, `v`), causing a mismatch between the reported label and the underlying server data.

This PR updates `unescapeEnumName` to decode `\0`, `\b`, `\f`, `\a`, and `\v` to their corresponding control characters, aligning with the server and matching `@clickhouse/datatype-parser` (`packages/datatype-parser/src/lexer.ts:107-136`). In particular, `\0` does not consume following digits, properly unescaping types such as `Enum8('a\012b' = 1)` to `a\x0012b`.

Fixes #1139.

## Checklist

- [x] Unit and integration tests covering the common scenarios were added
- [x] A human-readable changelog entry was added to every affected package's `CHANGELOG.md` (e.g. `packages/client-node/CHANGELOG.md`; a shared/common change updates both client packages — `client-node` and `client-web`; the root `CHANGELOG.md` is frozen)

title: test(upstream-sql-tests): turn off the runner's own retries
body:
## Summary

`scripts/run-upstream-tests.sh` now passes `--dont_retry_failures` to `tests/clickhouse-test`.

Without the flag, the upstream runner runs a failed test again when its output contains one of `MESSAGES_TO_RETRY` (for example "No such file or directory", "Permission denied", "Connection reset by peer", "(total) memory limit exceeded"), at most 3 times. When the test passes on a retry, the runner reports it as `OK` and the job is green. So a flaky test looks stable and can get into the allowlist. That is contrary to rule 5 of the harness `AGENTS.md` ("remove it ... rather than retrying"). With the flag, each failure fails the run.

Evidence, `tests/clickhouse-test` at the pinned `UPSTREAM_REF` (`c6428ebc`, v26.10.2.103-stable):

- `TestResult.check_if_need_retry` sets `need_retry` only if `not args.dont_retry_failures` (and the output matches `MESSAGES_TO_RETRY`, and `runs_count <= MAX_RETRIES`).
- The flag is defined after a `parse_known_args()` call, so `--help` does not list it, but the runner accepts it.

The same change was made in the C# harness after a review: https://github.com/ClickHouse/clickhouse-cs/pull/747.

No allowlist change, no client change (no CHANGELOG entry: the harness is not a published package).

## Test

In a local stack (server 26.10.4.207, upstream tests at the pin):

- A probe test that fails on its first run with "No such file or directory" on stderr and passes on the next run:
  - `python3 tests/clickhouse-test <probe>` (as on `main`): `[ OK ]`, "1 tests passed", exit 0. The failed first run shows only under "Some tests were restarted".
  - `run-upstream-tests.sh` with this change: `[ FAIL ]`, "Having 1 errors!", exit 1.
- `run-upstream-tests.sh --no-stateful` with `SHARD_INDEX=1 SHARD_TOTAL=10` (passthrough): 295 tests passed, exit 0.
- `bash -n` on the script; `prettier --check` on the README.

The `upstream-sql-tests` workflow of this PR runs the full allowlist of both backends with the flag.

title: fix(parseColumnType): validate DateTime64 precision and timezone syntax (#1127)
body:
Fixes #1127

### Description
In `parseColumnType` / `parseDateTime64Type` (`packages/client-common/src/parse/column_types.ts`), `DateTime64` precision was parsed from a single character at a fixed index (`columnType[DateTime64Prefix.length]`) and timezone was sliced using fixed offsets without validating token boundaries or syntax. As a result:
- `DateTime64(10)` was silently accepted as precision `1` with an empty string timezone.
- `DateTime64(12, 'UTC')` was silently accepted as precision `1` with timezone `"'UTC"` (retaining the opening quote).
- Unquoted or malformed timezones were not rejected.

### Changes
1. Require that `DateTime64(...)` ends with `)` and extract the parameter substring.
2. Validate precision token explicitly: verify it is a valid single integer within `[0 : 9]`. Reject out-of-range or multi-digit precision (e.g. `10`, `12`, `-1`, `01`, `foo`, `'`) with `ColumnTypeParseError("Invalid DateTime64 precision")`.
3. Validate timezone token: verify it is properly quoted (`'...'`), has minimum length 4 (matching shortest IANA timezone `GB`), and does not contain stray single quotes. Reject malformed timezones with `ColumnTypeParseError("Invalid DateTime64 type")`.
4. Add unit test coverage in `packages/client-common/__tests__/unit/parse_column_types_datetime.test.ts`.

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **Medium Risk**
> Stricter validation in shared type parsing can throw where malformed `DateTime64` strings were previously accepted silently, affecting `parseColumnType` consumers (e.g. RowBinary header parsing).
> 
> **Overview**
> **Tightens `DateTime64` parsing** in deprecated `parseDateTime64Type` so malformed type strings fail fast instead of being misread (e.g. `DateTime64(10)` no longer becomes precision `1`).
> 
> The parser now requires a closing `)`, reads the inner parameter list, and treats precision as a single integer in **0–9** (rejecting `10`, `12`, `-1`, `01`, non-numeric tokens). When a timezone is present, it must be a properly quoted `'...'` literal with minimum length and valid escaping; unquoted or stray-quote forms throw **`Invalid DateTime64 type`**.
> 
> Unit tests cover the new invalid cases; Node and Web **CHANGELOG** entries document the fix ([#1161]).
> 
> <sup>Reviewed by [Cursor Bugbot](https://cursor.com/bugbot) for commit 3fe8204cb3b11feed13e1bc4997786e2fa56324f. Bugbot is set up for automated code reviews on this repo. Configure [here](https://www.cursor.com/dashboard/bugbot).</sup>

title: feat(data_formatter): allow plain object input in TupleParam (#1107)
body:
Partially addresses #1107

### Description
When querying named `Tuple` columns (e.g. `Tuple(protocol UInt8, port UInt16)`), the values returned from `SELECT ... FORMAT JSONEachRow` are plain JavaScript objects (`{ protocol: 6, port: 80 }`).
Currently, passing a plain JS object in `query_params` routes through `formatObjectLikeParam`, which formats it as ClickHouse `Map` syntax (`{'protocol':6,'port':80}`). The server rejects this with code 27 `CANNOT_PARSE_INPUT_ASSERTION_FAILED` because a Map literal cannot be bound to a Tuple parameter.

To bind back named tuples, callers had to manually unpack properties into a positional array (`new TupleParam([6, 80])`), discarding field names.

### Changes
- Updated `TupleParam` constructor to accept both `readonly unknown[]` and `Record<string, unknown>`.
- For plain object inputs, values are extracted in property order via `Object.values(obj)`.
- Preserves backwards compatibility: array inputs continue to work identically, and bare objects without `TupleParam` continue to format as Maps.
- Added unit tests covering object inputs, empty objects, and invalid inputs in `packages/client-common/__tests__/unit/format_query_params.test.ts`.

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **Low Risk**
> Additive API change in query-parameter formatting with tests; array behavior unchanged, though tuple element order from objects follows JavaScript property order.
> 
> **Overview**
> **`TupleParam`** now accepts **plain JavaScript objects** in addition to arrays, so named tuple values from query results (e.g. `{ protocol: 6, port: 80 }`) can be bound back without manually building a positional array.
> 
> Object fields are turned into tuple element order via **`Object.values()`** and still serialize as a ClickHouse tuple literal `(v1, v2, …)` rather than Map syntax. **Array inputs are unchanged**; bare objects without `TupleParam` still format as Maps. Invalid constructor input (`null`, `undefined`, non-array/non-object) now **throws** with a clear message.
> 
> Unit tests cover object, empty object, and error cases; Node and Web **CHANGELOG** entries document the improvement ([#1162]).

title: ci: run the upstream SQL tests on a PR with the tests:run-core-sql label
body:
## Summary

`upstream-sql-tests.yml` (the core SQL test harness) runs nightly, by hand, and on pushes and PRs that change `tests/clickhouse-test-runner/**` or the workflow. A PR that changes only a client does not start it. This PR adds the `tests:run-core-sql` label, which runs the harness on any PR, as `tests:run-cloud` does for the Cloud tests.

- New workflow `upstream-sql-tests-label.yml`: it starts on `pull_request` `labeled`, calls `upstream-sql-tests.yml` (`uses: ./.github/workflows/upstream-sql-tests.yml`) when the label is `tests:run-core-sql`, and then removes the label. To run the tests again, add the label again.
- `upstream-sql-tests.yml` gets a `workflow_call:` trigger and one header comment. Nothing else changes in it. A second workflow is necessary because the `paths` filter of the `pull_request` trigger also applies to a `labeled` event.
- The trigger is `pull_request`, not `pull_request_target`: the tests need no secrets, and the code of a fork runs with a read-only token. That token cannot remove the label, so the `remove-label` job skips forks (the README says to remove the label by hand there).
- The calling job has `permissions: {}`, the same as the top-level `permissions` of `upstream-sql-tests.yml`. Only the separate `remove-label` job gets `pull-requests: write`, so the PR code never runs with a token that can write.
- In a called run, `github.event.inputs.upstream_ref` is empty, so the pinned `UPSTREAM_REF` applies.
- The label run has its own concurrency group (`github.workflow` is the name of the calling workflow), so it does not cancel a run that a push to the same PR started.
- The harness `README.md` (CI) documents the label.

The label exists in the repository now. The same label and workflow are in ClickHouse/clickhouse-cs#749.

No changelog entry: CI only, no change to a package.

## Checklist

- [x] Prettier 3.9.10 (`prettier --check` on the changed files), actionlint 1.7.12 (both workflows: no findings), zizmor 1.29.0 (new workflow: no findings).
- [x] The label run on this PR passes and removes the label: [run 44557508132](https://github.com/ClickHouse/clickhouse-js/actions/runs/44557508132) (`{passthrough, rowbinary} × 10` shards: all passed; then `remove-label`). The path-triggered run of the same PR ([run 44557496068](https://github.com/ClickHouse/clickhouse-js/actions/runs/44557496068)) ran at the same time, was not cancelled, and passed.

title: feat(client-native): add Node.js client over the native TCP protocol
body:
## Summary

This PR introduces `@clickhouse/client-native` (experimental `0.1.0`), a zero-dependency Node.js client for ClickHouse over the **native TCP protocol** (`tcp://host:9000`, `tcps://host:9440`) with the same public API as `@clickhouse/client`.

### Motivation

We are migrating high-volume workloads from Python to Node.js/TypeScript in an infrastructure setup where ClickHouse access goes exclusively over the native TCP port (HTTP is not exposed) and processes large amounts of data. Keeping API parity with `@clickhouse/client` lets users switch transports by changing only the package import and connection URL.

### What's Included

- **Drop-in API compatibility:** `query`, `command`, `insert`, `exec`, and `ping`, plus connection pooling, TLS / mutual TLS, query parameters, ClickHouse settings, and `AbortSignal` support.
- **Protocol & type support:** Native block decoding across ClickHouse column types (including `Variant`, `Dynamic`, and `JSON` wire forms; excluding `AggregateFunction`, `QBit`, and deprecated `Object('json')`), preserving raw bytes for non-UTF-8 `String` values.
- **HTTP-compatible formatting:** Formats `Native` blocks into `JSON*`, `CSV*`, and `TabSeparated*` outputs matching the HTTP interface byte-for-byte, respecting server output settings.
- **Inserts:** Encodes JSON-format row arrays and streams into `Native` blocks (16,384-row batches) with server-matching `DEFAULT`, null, and range-clamping behavior; streams raw non-JSON formats (`CSV`, `TabSeparated`, `Parquet`, etc.) to the server.
- **Compression:** Bidirectional `lz4` and `zstd` block compression (up to 1 MiB frames) with CityHash128 v1.0.2 in WebAssembly and a JS fallback.
- **Minimal shared changes:** `packages/client-common` accepts transport-specific URL protocol defaults (`url_options`) and logs progress-header warnings only on HTTP URLs. Existing behavior in `@clickhouse/client` and `@clickhouse/client-web` is unchanged.
- **CI, release & repo skills:** Workflows for unit/integration/TLS matrices, tarball `dist` checks, curated upstream SQL tests (`--client=native`), version bumping, and npm publishing, plus updated contributor docs and repo skills (`packages/AGENTS.md`, `.claude/skills/*`, `.claude/agents/docs-drift-reviewer.md`) to keep `client-node` and `client-native` aligned.

### Performance & Validation

Because this PR is large, we invested heavily in correctness and performance testing before opening it:

- **Runtime compatibility:** Automated and manual testing across all supported Node.js versions (Node 22, 24, and 26, including pre-`zlib.zstd` Node 22.14) as well as **Bun 1.4.4**.
- **Performance optimization & E2E benchmarking:** Profiled hot paths and added targeted optimizations—such as direct `Native`-to-JSON object construction (skipping intermediate text serialization/parsing in `ResultSet.json()`), fast-path binary-to-JSON row writers for common integer/boolean/UTF-8 string blocks, buffer reuse, and WASM CityHash128. Benchmarked end-to-end against the Python native TCP client across varied query and insert load scenarios to confirm there are no performance regressions after migrating from Python.
- **Test suites run:**
  - `npm run typecheck` — passed
  - `npm run lint` — passed
  - `npm run test:native:unit` — passed (7 test files, 204 tests)
  - `npm run test:node:unit` — passed (45 test files, 443 tests)
  - `npm run test:native:dist` — passed
  - Native integration, TLS, HTTP byte-for-byte parity suites, and curated upstream SQL tests verified against ClickHouse in Docker across Node 22/24/26 and Bun 1.4.4 (not re-run in this local draft step without Docker running; covered by `.github/workflows/tests-native.yml` and `.github/workflows/upstream-sql-tests.yml`).

### Benchmark comparison (`@clickhouse/client-native` vs `@clickhouse/client`)

Indicative results from [`benchmarks/native/`](benchmarks/native/README.md) (macOS, Node.js `v26.13.1`, ClickHouse `26.10.1.1562`, loopback `127.0.0.1`, `iterations=7`, `warmup=2`):

| Scenario | `@clickhouse/client` (HTTP) | `@clickhouse/client-native` (TCP) | Native vs HTTP | CPU/op (HTTP → Native) | JS Alloc/op (HTTP → Native) |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Sequential `SELECT 1` (200 reqs) | 497.0 req/s (2.00 ms) | **2.3k req/s (0.43 ms)** | **4.59x** | 0.638 → **0.263 ms** | 93.1 → **57.6 KiB** |
| Concurrent pool (16×25 reqs) | 5.7k req/s | **9.7k req/s** | **1.69x** | 0.219 → **0.157 ms** | 75.9 → **46.7 KiB** |
| `JSONEachRow` `.json()` (100k rows) | 1.50M rows/s | **3.86M rows/s** | **2.58x** | 68.7 → **49.2 ms** | 50.0 → **33.5 MiB** |
| `JSONEachRow` `.stream()` (200k rows, binary fast path) | 4.85M rows/s | **10.54M rows/s** | **2.17x** | 34.5 → **23.7 ms** | 63.1 → **22.2 MiB** |
| Compressed `.json()` (200k rows, LZ4 vs gzip) | 1.83M rows/s | **6.58M rows/s** | **3.60x** | 119.5 → **45.1 ms** | 91.1 → **35.0 MiB** |
| Structured `JSONEachRow` insert (100k rows, LZ4 vs gzip) | 745.1k rows/s | **1.20M rows/s** | **1.61x** | 50.7 → **40.9 ms** | 21.5 → **7.12 MiB** |
| Raw CSV stream insert (1M rows, 24.3 MiB) | 159.3 MiB/s | 157.6 MiB/s | 0.99x | 8.42 → **5.95 ms** | 698 → **243 KiB** |
| Complex types: `Tuple`/`Array`/`JSON`/TZ (50k rows) | 279.6k rows/s | **355.6k rows/s** | **1.27x** | 68.9 → **67.0 ms** | **36.6** → 41.0 MiB |
| Binary `JSON` paths (50k rows, 8 keys/row) | 194.2k rows/s | **266.4k rows/s** | **1.37x** | **37.6** → 45.8 ms | **23.8** → 30.2 MiB |
| Early `ResultSet.close()` on 50M-row query + recovery | 77.9 req/s (12.8 ms) | **213.9 req/s (4.67 ms)** | **2.75x** | **4.37** → 10.3 ms | **928** → 1016 KiB |

To reproduce locally:

```sh
npm run build
NODE_OPTIONS="--expose-gc" npx tsx benchmarks/native/index.ts
```

### Design Notes

- **Blast radius on existing packages:** Changes outside `packages/client-native` are ~60 lines in `packages/client-common` (optional `url_options` for `tcp:`/`tcps:` schemes, default ports 9000/9440 on tracing spans, and scoping the HTTP progress-header warning to HTTP URLs) plus a 2-line explicit `HttpURLOptions` wire-up in `packages/client-node`. `@clickhouse/client` and `@clickhouse/client-web` retain identical runtime behavior.
- **Why a separate `@clickhouse/client-native` package (experimental `0.x`):** Follows the workspace split (`client-node` / `client-web`), keeps the Native wire codec, formatter, and compression code out of HTTP client bundles, and lets the TCP implementation iterate under `0.x` semver without risking stability of `@clickhouse/client`.
- **Supply chain, native addons & WASM:** Zero runtime npm dependencies and no C++/N-API native addons (installs cleanly without `node-gyp`). LZ4 is pure TypeScript, ZSTD uses Node's built-in `node:zlib` (`>= 22.15.0`), and CityHash128 v1.0.2 is constructed directly from readable TypeScript opcode helpers in `src/compression/cityhash.ts` (no opaque `.wasm` binary blob), with an automatic pure-JS fallback (`cityhash_js.ts`, e.g. under `--jitless`) verified against it in unit tests.
- **Security & resource bounds:** Compressed frame headers enforce ClickHouse's `DBMS_MAX_COMPRESSED_SIZE` before allocating memory, LZ4 decompression checks all read/write bounds, WASM linear memory is released after large hashes, and `client.close()` / `AbortSignal` cleanly tear down active sockets, TLS handshakes, and pending stream reads.
- **Client-side formatting vs. server nuances:** Because the native protocol transfers typed `Native` blocks rather than pre-rendered text, the client formats `JSON*`, `CSV*`, and `TabSeparated*` locally (verified byte-for-byte against the HTTP interface in `compare_http.test.ts` and `output_bytes.test.ts`). Where server input parsing varies across ClickHouse releases or relies on server-side expression evaluation (e.g., per-row `DEFAULT` expressions, `Dynamic` date string inference, or `JSONStrings` complex columns), `insert()` automatically falls back to sending those batches for server-side parsing. All HTTP vs. TCP differences (stateful connection sessions, non-atomic multi-batch inserts, Node time zone data) are documented in `packages/client-native/README.md`.
- **Splitting / incremental review:** Workflows for publishing (`publish-client-native.yml`, `bump-version.yml`) are gated on the `release` branch and manual approval, so merging to `main` will not publish anything automatically. If maintainers prefer reviewing this in smaller PRs (e.g., `client-common` hook → core protocol/codec → client & CI), we are happy to split it.

### AI Usage Disclosure

In line with [`AI_POLICY.md`](./AI_POLICY.md): most of the implementation was generated with Fable 5.2 following a manually reviewed and edited design plan. Each iteration was cross-reviewed across independent models (Astra 6.2 and Gemini 4 Carbon) and manually reviewed, refined, and validated by us end-to-end before submission.

Happy to walk through any module in detail or adjust scope based on maintainer feedback!

- [x] A human-readable changelog entry was added to every affected package's `CHANGELOG.md` (e.g. `packages/client-node/CHANGELOG.md`; a shared/common change updates both client packages — `client-node` and `client-web`; the root `CHANGELOG.md` is frozen)
- [ ] For significant changes, documentation in https://github.com/ClickHouse/clickhouse-docs was updated with further explanations or tutorials

> **Overview**
> Adds **`@clickhouse/client-native` (0.1.0, experimental)** — a zero-dependency Node.js client that speaks ClickHouse’s native TCP protocol (`tcp://` / `tcps://`) while exposing the same **`createClient` API** as `@clickhouse/client` (`query`, `command`, `insert`, `exec`, `ping`, pooling, TLS, compression, cancellation).
